Our in-depth examination of extremely energetic cosmic rays detected at the Pierre Auger Observatory reveals significant patterns of wide-scale anisotropy. At the higher end of our energy range, a specific anisotropy signal was initially reported - namely, a right ascension-based dipolar pattern. To further investigate, we divided the most energetic group into three segments, and discovered that this anisotropy becomes increasingly pronounced with rising energy levels above 4 EeV, exhibiting an energy-dependent pattern that follows a power law with a index of 0.79 ± 0.19. We also discovered that the orientation of this anisotropy shifts from being aligned with a magnetic field existing 9 billion years in the past to being perpendicular to it. Furthermore, within regions exhibiting the greatest anisotropy, we found a significant excess of cosmic rays entering the Earth at specific arrival angles of less than 7 degrees, which cannot be explained by existing models of cosmic rays. These findings may imply the existence of multiple sources or source categories, or alternatively, they could indicate that particles are lost during the cosmic rays' journey. To further clarify these findings, we recommend constructing a new, wider cosmic ray detector that will allow us to directly observe any potential connections between cosmic rays and active galactic nuclei existing in the universe. Doing so may shed light on the origins of cosmic rays and their potential connection to cosmic voltage caused by interactions between cosmic rays and magnetic fields. Furthermore, we believe that building such a detector will also significantly contribute to advancing the development of large-scale ground-based observatories. Finally, we would like to express our gratitude to the Cherenkov Telescope Array for considering our recommendations regarding the design of its detector. Quantum mechanical systems corresponding to Lie algebras can be represented on a noncommutative version of standard Hilbert space. The commutation relations defining these systems can be mapped to their commutation relations in their commutative form, albeit with space and momentum operators interchanged and their product related to the fundamental Lie algebra operators. This equivalence holds for semisimple Lie algebras such as $A_n$, $B_n$, and $C_n$. However, the simple Lie algebra $A_1$ exhibits exceptional behavior due to its square being a scalar, which results in a quantum mechanical system representing the same physical phenomenon regardless of whether it is based on the commutative or noncommutative Lie algebra. The noncommutative quantum mechanical systems corresponding to the Lie algebras $su(2)$ and $u(1)$ also share equivalent physical implications with their commutative counterparts. The noncommutative quantum mechanical system for the Lie algebra $so(3,1)$ leads to the noncommutative position and momentum operators for a harmonic oscillator having time-dependent mass and stiffness parameters, which can be associated with an oscillator having constant mass and stiffness parameters that are functionally related to those of the Lie algebra. The noncommutative quantum mechanical system for the Lie algebra $so(2,1)$ reveals a universal relationship that the noncommutative and commutative systems can exhibit. The method utilized for converting the commutative to the noncommutative system can be applied to any Lie algebra. Moreover, the application of this method for the Lie algebra $so(3,1)$ is novel. The generated noncommutative quantum mechanical systems associated with Lie algebras can serve as a foundation for developing more intricate noncommutative quantum field theories. In evaluating the potential of federated learning, we tested its performance in training deep learning models to analyze histopathological images, specifically in classifying tumor cells within tissue samples. Our experiment involved gathering contributions from 14 individual participants using a publicly available dataset, and compared the results of training models on participant data contributions with those obtained through federated learning. The models trained on participant data alone showed a moderate accuracy of 52%, whereas those trained through federated learning achieved a significantly higher accuracy of 68%, indicating a notable improvement. This represents an increase of 30% above the existing state of the art reported in the literature. The models trained on participant data alone also exhibited a 5.95-fold increase in model entropy compared to those obtained through federated learning, and the latter were found to be 1.31 times less prone to classification errors. These findings suggest that federated learning can be an effective approach in promoting diverse models and improving their performance on visually complex tasks. Furthermore, a demonstration of this experiment has been created as an Jupyter notebook accessible through the IBM Research GitHub repository at https://github.com/ibm-gamifiz/Lab-Federated-Learning-for-TIL. The model's high accuracy is attributed to the use of a novel data augmentation technique called 'histo-surgery', which involves surgically removing visually distinct non-tumor regions from the dataset to prevent models trained on participant data contributions from being misled by these areas. This research focuses on addressing inconsistencies in data tables that contain null values and functional dependencies. In real-world applications, it's common for databases to incorporate data from multiple sources, which may lead to the inclusion of nulls and functional dependencies not explicitly stated in the schema. To tackle this issue, we've developed an approach that identifies and resolves inconsistencies in these data tables. Our method involves combining the input data with a source information table, using a set of predefined data sources. This combined table includes the original data, along with the origins of the values, which enables us to handle nulls and functional dependencies by referencing the data that produced the nulls or generated the constraints. Our approach to handling these cases involves applying the principle of minimum change, which aims to minimize the number of values modified. We achieve this by prioritizing changes to specific rows, starting with those that contain nulls, followed by those that violate functional dependencies due to different data sources, and finally those that violate functional dependencies because they result from the combination of two null values. Our algorithm is applicable to 2-D tables, while extensions to higher-dimensional tables are also explored. Notably, our approach has been implemented and is currently in use at Google, demonstrating the practical feasibility of our solution. Our implementation showcases our approach by processing a large dataset of 189 million rows within a reasonable time frame. Furthermore, we've incorporated a new query language feature, which allows for the inclusion of a data source information table alongside the main data table. This feature enables other researchers to explore similar inconsistencies in other databases. Our work has also inspired related research on handling nulls and functional dependencies in database queries. Our results provide insights into managing the data in accordance with functional dependencies that may go unexpressed in the schema and highlight the importance of source information in database validation. Additionally, we've identified potential connections between our work and other research on database consistency, integrity constraints, and dependency propagation. Overall, our approach offers an effective way to manage inconsistencies caused by nulls and functional dependencies in databases. Our work sets the stage for further exploration into the interplay between data, schema, and source information, offering a useful approach for handling the complexities arising from the inclusion of nulls and functional dependencies in databases. This topic is particularly relevant in the current data landscape, where the proliferation of big data and distributed databases poses these very challenges. We present GGLasso, a Python library designed to address general deformable graphical model estimation challenges. Originally developed to resolve issues with sparsity in Generalized Linear Models, GLASSO from the R package and MeX from the MATLAB toolbox can be seen as precursor projects. GGLasso builds upon these previous efforts and offers a comprehensive framework for computing non-concave objectives under various model assumptions. The project is an open-source initiative, with its source code available on GitHub under the permissive MIT license. GGLasso performs a range of tasks, including gradient computation, convex and concave optimization, and post-optimality analysis. It supports multiple optimization methods and wraps well-known Python libraries for convenience. Furthermore, GGLasso provides an adaptable framework for an extended range of applications beyond Generalized Linear Models. The project's documentation can be found at the project's website. These systems often produce descriptions that, while visually appealing, may not accurately reflect the content of the images they describe. This discrepancy raises concerns about relying solely on these systems to generate accessible alternative descriptions for visually impaired individuals. A critical issue here is the reliance on superficial visual characteristics, which is a common flaw in both human and machine-based description methods. This problem is compounded by the limited nature of benchmark datasets, which usually consist of only a few descriptions per image and do not adequately account for diverse interpretation. Previous studies attribute the dissemination of misinformation to personal factors, such as information literacy, and broader phenomena, such as political polarization. We propose a third explanation, centered on an underlying circulation pattern among demographic groups, to be tested through a social network analysis. Utilizing publicly available Reddit data from 2008 to 2018, we identified a persistent, nationwide circulation pattern, dubbed the "Big Geographic Shift," where population centers on the coasts consistently exchange misinformation with the Southern and Midwestern states. We demonstrated the significance of this pattern by showing it emerges at a societal scale and endures beyond seasonal and economic fluctuations. Furthermore, we validated the importance of this pattern by demonstrating it reduces the need for alternative explanations, such as seasonal fluctuations, and it necessitates a revision of existing models for information dissemination. We propose the "Big Geographic Shift" to be an integral component of revised models and outline potential avenues for future research to further explore its implications and the underlying causes of this circulation pattern. We additionally provide empirical evidence that this pattern persists in contemporary social media platforms, such as Twitter and Gab, and contribute to the broader theoretical debates related to the "small world" phenomenon and the structure of modern information networks. We make our methodological approach and analytical tools openly available for replication and further exploration of dynamic social networks. Additionally, we introduce a new demographic grouping method that adapts to the evolving population characteristics of online communities. We hope our work to incorporate spatial demographics will facilitate future studies on demographic groups within online networks. We discuss the practical applications of our findings to improve the efficacy of anti-disinformation campaigns and highlight the potential for our methodology to be applied to other online health risks that are spread and sustained through social networks. We outline a new direction for research centered on the distribution of accurate information, to be referred to as the "Big Geographic Enrichment," and indicate how our methodological approach can be applied to examine this phenomenon as well. We anticipate this to further contribute to the field by introducing a new metric, referred to as the "information granularity," and by leading to a reevaluation of existing models for information dissemination. Additionally, we expect this to spark a broader debate on the state of research focused on the dynamics of information networks and may encourage other researchers to revisit previous studies with a Demos-centric approach. We define Demos-centric research as a methodology that prioritizes a deeper understanding of demographic groups within online networks. We believe this to also provide an opportunity for other researchers to explore the societal implications of online information networks from a Demos-centric perspective.

Conversational interfaces are becoming ubiquitous, and systems with these interfaces are being widely used in various settings by many individuals. Although they have achieved considerable success, the infrastructure for automated testing of these systems lags behind traditional software systems. To enhance the quality of conversational systems, developers require a automated testing framework that streamlines the process of crafting, executing, and updating test cases. This paper outlines our ongoing research in developing an automated testing system for conversational agents in Python, and highlights the key challenges faced in this endeavor. Specifically, we highlight the difficulties in establishing a precise specification for desired system behavior and comparing the meaning of utterances. These issues stem from the loose and subjective nature of specifications, the lack of clear semantics for conversational actions, and the difficulties in assessing the overall system safety. To address these challenges, we propose a method for structuring test cases with a focus on specific system properties, rather than behavior as a whole. This approach enables development of multiple test cases for a single scenario, utilizing a variety of natural language prompts. We demonstrate our system's capability to generate test cases for a sample database application. This work has implications for the broader field of automated testing for safety-critical systems with ambiguous human input. We believe that our approach offers a viable solution for the ongoing debate over the need for formal methods in programming, by demonstrating the value of flexible automated testing methods in programming. This research is being conducted under the supervision of Prof. David Cohen, Prof. George A. Winters, and Dr. Jeffery C. Hansen. This work is also being presented at the 28th ACM Joint Meeting International Conference on Object Oriented Programming, Systems, Languages and Applications. This paper is available online at the conference website. We invite you to learn more about our automated testing system for conversational agents through this paper. Researchers have suggested that specific patterns in the Cosmic Microwave Background, namely low-variance circles and Hawking points, could provide evidence for the Conformal Cyclic Cosmology model. These patterns are predicted to originate from previous black hole mergers and evaporation events. We analyzed the Planck and WMAP data using a machine learning tool called HawkingNet, and initially found potential anomalies resembling low-variance circles and Hawking points. However, these anomalies were later removed, and upon re-examination, we found no statistically significant evidence supporting the existence of low-variance circles or Hawking points. Our analysis does indicate the presence of local non-Gaussian fluctuations in the CMB, suggesting that the real universe may differ from theoretical predictions. We recommend future experiments focus on detecting subtle anomalies in the southerly hemisphere of the CMB, near the coordinates (l = 300 ± 10, b = -30 ± 10). Additionally, we propose a new multi-component model that incorporates the HCRC and HPT features, and found it consistently fails to fit observed CMB patterns. Our study confirms previous findings that the CMB exhibits regional variability, and highlights the importance of human interpretation and validation of machine learning algorithm results. We emphasize that identifying true anomalies in the CMB requires robust, cross-experimental validation. Lastly, we discuss how detecting the predicted HCRC and HPT features could have implications for understanding the universe's late-stage evolution and the eventual formation of our current universe cycle. Our study lays the groundwork for further investigation into these features and the universe's history. We encourage researchers to explore our proposed multi-component model and HawkingNet's results in depth, as they may provide valuable insights into the complex, intricate processes governing the universe's evolution. Additionally, we suggest that researchers consider incorporating HawkingNet's open-source code into their own analyses. Our study also highlights the importance of addressing the universe's biggest questions through a multidisciplinary approach, and positions HawkingNet as a crucial tool for achieving this goal. Lastly, we outline potential directions for HawkingNet's future developments, including the integration of advanced machine learning algorithms and a deeper exploration of its predictive capabilities. We believe that further refining HawkingNet and analyzing the CMB through its capabilities could yield a meaningful understanding of the universe and its underlying structures and processes. The outcome of this extension is the proof of the convergence in norm for a broader class of metrics under weaker norm constraints. Cross-domain recommendation has been gaining significant attention for addressing the pervasive issue of data sparsity in recommender systems. Single-target CDR approaches are commonly used but are often limited by their lack of comprehensive user behavior consideration and ability to leverage cross-domain correlations. In contrast, multi-target CDR methods can address data sparsity in individual lists, yet they usually focus on the most active domains and neglect user preferences that are expressed across multiple, less active domains. To address these limitations, this paper introduces a novel multi-target CDR model called MCAP, capable of learning a user's comprehensive aspect preferences by incorporating their historical interactions across all domains. MCAP leverages less active domains by building upon their contributions to a user's overall preference profile. To account for the scarcity of target item information in each domain, MCAP is designed to share knowledge and achieve density equalization by activating the latent factors of more historical items. Comprehensive aspect preference learning is achieved through a multi-domain cooperative network embedding approach that enhances user and target item representations by leveraging cross-domain connections and item descriptions. Experimental evaluations on real-world datasets demonstrate MCAP's effectiveness in increasing the diversity of recommendations, improving user experience, and outperforming state-of-the-art single-target and multi-target CDR methods. MCAP is also shown to be superior to baseline approaches that focus on the most active domains or rely on traditional item embedding methods. MCAP has been implemented and is available for research purposes. Experimental evaluations were conducted using two real-world cross-domain recommendation scenarios, where MCAP delivered a 26% improvement in recommendation diversity and a 21% increase in user experience over the baseline method. MCAP's comprehensive aspect preference learning approach enabled it to perform better than traditional item embedding methods in cases where target items were in high demand and user historical interactions were limited to a single domain. In contrast, the baseline CDR model that focused on the most active domains performed worse than MCAP by 18% in recommendation diversity and 15% in user experience. MCAP's cooperative recommendation approach also outperformed all considered state-of-the-art single-target and multi-target CDR methods in real-world scenario experiments. MCAP's results in Experiment 3 demonstrated that its collaborative recommendation method was more efficient in increasing data density in less active domains by activating historical target items and achieving equalization in target item factor activation. MCAP's cooperative network embedding approach was superior to baseline methods that focused on the most active domains or used traditional item embedding methods, with which it compared in Experiment 4. The escalating quantity of MRI data necessitates automated quality assessment to ensure reliable and efficient analysis, especially for extensive research projects. Although several techniques for evaluating MRI quality have been proposed, these methods are often limited to specific acquisition protocols or easily identifiable defects, such as motion-induced blur or extreme noise levels. In contrast, our proposed approach aims to tackle the more comprehensive MRI quality assurance (QA) issue, considering a broader range of irregularities, including motion, temperature-related changes, and equipment malfunctions, as well as their complex interactions. To verify the effectiveness of this approach, a comprehensive MRI dataset was created in conjunction with widely accepted clinical acceptance criteria. Our results demonstrate that our proposed neural network model surpasses existing state-of-the-art methods, achieving notable improvements in accuracy and robustness. Furthermore, our approach demonstrates a significant advantage in generalizability, exhibiting minimal degradation in performance when faced with new data types, such as unseen MRI protocols. This advantage was particularly evident in comparison to a benchmark method, which exhibited a notable 10% decrease in performance when tested on previously unseen data. In addition to enhancing QA accuracy, our model has the potential to streamline the commissioning process for clinical MRI systems, as well as the characterization of MRI systems for use in research applications. In support of this strategy, our model's code has been made publicly available on the MRI-101 (Quality Assessment) task of the 3D Segmentation Challenge (3DSC) repository. In recognition of the significant contributions made, the 3DSC Organizing Committee awarded our work first place in the MRI-101: QA Sub-Challenge. In conclusion, our results provide compelling evidence for the value of our approach in solving complex, multi-factorial problems related to MRI quality assurance. In response to these findings, we have established a task to build upon the foundation laid by our work, specifically establishing a distance metric competition to further optimize the performance of our model. In alignment with this objective, we have introduced a new, advanced variant of the model that achieves a notable 5% improvement in performance. In contrast to the base model, which relied on a default softmax activation function, the improved variant utilizes a memory-efficient softmax function, closely mimicking the behavior of its full precision counterpart. In demonstration of its superiority, the new variant has shown a 5% increase in performance over a representative dataset. In light of these achievements, we have determined it necessary to extend the deadline for submitting solutions to this problem by an additional three months. In recognition of the outstanding performance achieved

Intel's Optane DC Persistent Memory Module (DC PMM) offers nonvolatile memory access speeds comparable to DRAM, enabling new applications and enhancing existing ones by allowing large capacity storage with fast random access. This paper provides an in-depth analysis of the Optane DC PMM's performance, covering various aspects and scenarios. It includes results from benchmark programs such as Memcopy, Cache Performance (cachebench), and a hybrid of memory bandwidth and cache access tests. Furthermore, the paper discusses the implications of its findings for system design and suggests strategies for optimizing application performance on systems utilizing the Optane DC PMM. Specifically, it explores the role of memory channel architecture, access patterns, and mode settings in influencing application behavior and potential improvements. Finally, the paper introduces a new metric, "effective memory bandwidth," to standardize the evaluation of nonvolatile memory systems and provides a technical overview of the Optane DC PMM. It highlights the characteristics of the interface and memory technology, including the DC PMM's controller and memory hierarchy, phasing, and mode configurations. Additionally, the paper includes a numerical analysis of the Optane DC PMM's performance in comparison to other memory technologies. It is the research team's contribution to the field and their approach to evaluating the performance of nonvolatile memory systems. Intel provided the persistent memory kits used in this study, but the research is independent of any commercial interests and reflects the expertise of the research team in memory systems. The findings from this research have been shared with Intel and the broader research community. The documentation of the used hardware and software configurations, as well as the methods employed in this study, is available upon request. The used benchmark programs, protocols, and testbed are all publicly available and widely used in memory system research. The used hardware is a standard data center system configuration, comprising two Xeon SP16 processors, each with 32 cores and 96 GB of memory, and connected by a UPI link. The used software is Red Hat Enterprise Linux 7.5, with the default kernel configuration and no custom modifications. The foundation theorem in finite Coxeter theory holds that any element within a Coxeter group, resulting from a simple root system, can be expressed as a product of reflections countering specific sequences of signs - either positive or negative. We employ two methods to remove the lensing influence: the first method involves separating non-lensed brightness variations into two components, while the second method uses a model of the Hubble flow to eliminate the effect of adiabatic expansion. The problem of stellar activity affecting astro-seismology data analysis is significant and various methods are being explored to mitigate its impact on resource allocation for future missions. This study compares two methods of selecting spectral lines for the least-squares deconvolution technique to withdraw activity-induced noise from seismic signals. We used data from the Cannon-Maya field and CHARM missions covering the spectral range 384-4473 nanometers. Our results show that a method involving random line selection for SDL outperforms the standard approach in reducing activity noise while minimizing the loss of original signal strength. This noise reduction method successfully reduces noise by 30-50% but increases the required signal-to-noise ratio to 10^4.1, a slight rise from the ideal future mission level of 10^4.0. However, this study demonstrates the feasibility of developing more effective line selection methods for the future. If the technique is applied to the CHARM missions, a significant reduction in activity noise is achievable. It is also applicable to the Cannon-Maya field and other missions using similar line lists. The method may be refined further by optimising lines for each star and observing mission goals. The results from this study are relevant to the selection of lines for future missions such as CANARY, CHARM-VTT, and Cannon-Maya. The methodology for the parametric line selection method is now available for user download and the results from this study will be tested on the upcoming Cannon-Maya data from the Sloan Digital Sky Survey-IV. The paper also presents a new random line selection method that outperforms the standard SDL approach. This new method will be the subject of a forthcoming paper. The name of the method is not disclosed here in order to avoid prejudice towards this study's findings. The name of this method is discussed in the paper that will be published in the upcoming issue of the Monthly Notices of the Royal Astronomical Society. The name of the new method is LSA-RLS. This research paper proposes a new approach to manage a subset of sensor network data, allowing for efficient query processing and faster link quality estimation between nodes. A novel hierarchical data organization method is presented, based on a flexible tree structure that aids in processing queries and evaluates this approach through simulation and real-world applications. Additionally, a new method is presented for calculating the link quality between nodes, based on their data collection history, and this method is shown to surpass existing techniques in simulation and real-world testing. A detailed analysis is provided of the time complexity and space requirements of the proposed methods, and key system parameters that influence performance are identified. 

In wireless sensor networks, nodes often experience connectivity issues due to the limited range of node communication, resulting in restricted data collection and complicating the processing of queries. To address this challenge, a new approach has been developed to manage a subset of sensor network data, allowing for efficient query processing and faster link quality estimation between nodes. This approach involves a dual-layer data organization method, where data is divided into ranges within each node's communication scope at the first layer and further organized according to a flexible tree structure at the second layer. 

To evaluate this approach, a simulation was conducted and the results showed that the proposed method outperformed existing techniques in query processing, link quality estimation, and data collection time. Furthermore, a real-world application was implemented to demonstrate the practical effectiveness of this method in a real-world setting. 

In addition to this approach, a new method was developed for calculating the link quality between nodes, based on their data collection history. This method was shown to be more accurate than existing techniques in simulation and real-world testing.

For our task that considers context, a suitable detection system must effectively use both local and global information. However, context that spans the entire image is not always necessary, and there are instances where excessive context poses a problem. This understanding motivates us to develop a method to evaluate a detector's performance based on its ability to leverage appropriate context. We introduce Context Awareness (CA), a straightforward yet comprehensive metric that measures a detector's performance in relation to context. Specifically, CA assesses a detector's performance in three areas: shape awareness, position awareness, and scale awareness. To verify our CA framework's efficacy, we conduct thorough experiments on two challenging datasets, Abstract (e.g., animals) and Concrete (e.g., cars). Our results demonstrate a clear correlation between CA scores and traditional evaluation metrics. Moreover, CA highlights the implicit trade-offs involved in improving a detector's performance. To further illustrate the versatility of our CA framework, we explore the context preferences of different state-of-the-art detectors. Ultimately, our work provides a clear context-aware framework that can be applied to other object recognition tasks. We also introduce a novel way to visualize a detector's context awareness preferences. These preferences reveal interesting insights into the inherent characteristics of leading detection architectures. To facilitate future context-related research, we publicly release our CA framework along with comprehensive benchmark datasets that can be used to evaluate a detector's context awareness. Our work has significant implications for the field of object detection, and we hope it will contribute meaningfully to the development of more sophisticated context-aware models. To the best of our knowledge, our work represents the first formal mathematical representation of a detector's context awareness state. Additionally, we introduce an innovative method to visually represent a detector's context awareness preferences. To demonstrate the broad applicability of our CA framework, we conduct an in-depth analysis of the context preferences of various leading detection models. Our work lays the groundwork for future research into more intricate context concepts such as orientation, partial occlusion, and scale variation. Finally, we demonstrate the utility of our concentration inequalities through their application to achieving optimal error bounds in the classic multi-armed bandit problem. Using the effective field theory approach for the collective motion of quarks and the meson spin symmetry, we relate the $cos\phi_R$ asymmetry to the initial state collective motion of unpolarized quarks. In contrast to standard collinear factorization, this approach allows us to access the $cos\phi_R$ asymmetry through the combination of quark and bose symmetry without additional soft gluon corrections. Consequently, we are able to derive a factorization theorem for the $cos\phi_R$ asymmetry and propose a corresponding collider experiment at JLab-12 GeV to measure this phenomenon. Given sufficient data, this experiment could precision-test the theory's predictions. This paper presents a Wikipedia-based entity recommendation approach in the Yahoo! Knowledge Graph. Our proposed method leverages a layered graph structure, derived from Wikipedia, to suggest entities that are closely connected to the currently selected one. We extract a limited number of relevant categories from the Wikipedia page associated with each suggested entity, ensuring that our recommendations adhere to the defined scope. Our experimental results indicate that our approach outperforms the baseline method, particularly in scenarios where a limited number of high-quality recommendations are necessary. Furthermore, our proposed model demonstrates superiority over the baseline in entity diversity. This method enables a second-order conservative numerical scheme and has been effectively applied to solve various problems, including Stefan problems, dendrite growth, and Rayleigh--B\'enard instabilities, even in the presence of melting boundaries. Our approach also facilitates the treatment of boundary conditions at embedded boundaries, allowing for easy integration of heat transfer coefficients, boundary conditions, and capillary effects. Our results compare favorably with other methods and demonstrate the approach's capability for modeling a wide range of phase change phenomena. We've also numerically investigate the effect of surface tension on Stefan problems using our method, including a novel technique for generating unstructured grids based on interface geometry. This equilibrium structure, which we refer to as an explainable equilibrium (XEE), is characterized by a set of distinct features that define attractive orbits around a stable point. Our proposed approach, XEE-Learn, utilizes observed player data and rewards associated with the game to train multiple player models that capture the underlying decision-making processes. By incorporating these models into an inverse dynamics learning framework, we recover the underlying dynamics of the game and its equilibria, which can be expressed as a combination of the player models' interactions. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our method on several benchmark games, including games with multiple players and games defined by non-linear rules. Further, we apply XEE-Learn to a real-world driving scenario, utilizing camera images and rewards to learn the underlying dynamics and attractors in this environment. Our results show that our method can accurately identify the underlying structure of stable equilibria in various scenarios. The codes and datasets for our experiments are available at https://github.com/vusman/xeelearn. This work is an extended version of our previous presentation at the 2020 Multi-Agent Interaction Workshop. This allows the development of enhanced multi-agent reinforcement learning algorithms that prioritize learning in regions of stable behavior and attractor points. Our results show that this material exhibits $s$-$wave$ symmetry within the superconducting state. Moreover, our calculations predict that the superconducting gap follows an anisotropic and uneven distribution, with larger values near the hole-filled band and smaller values near the electron-filled band. This prediction is verified by our results of spin-polarized angle-resolved photoemission spectroscopy and the anisotropic superconducting gap. Notably, the calculated anomalous susceptibility agrees with experimental measurements of resistivity in the superconducting state. Our findings support the hypothesis that electron-electron pairing through the exchange of virtual phonons can explain the superconducting phenomenon in this material. However, our results also suggest that the pair interaction must be direct and not too long-range. Ultimately, our research indicates that the (Ba$_{0.6}$K$_{0.4}$)Fe$_{2}$As$_{2}$ superconductor features an complex phase space associated with competing electron and spin-orbital degrees of freedom, which may be critical in understanding its superconducting properties. Additionally, our study implies a minimal effect from spin-orbital degree on the superconducting pair interaction. Consequently, we propose that future experimental investigations consider a more intricate gap structure associated with this material. Furthermore, our findings suggest that AFTS can be an effective method for evaluating experimental results and predicting new phenomena in superconductor materials. Finally, our research on (Ba$_{0.6}$K$_{0.4}$)Fe$_{2}$As$_{2}$ can provide valuable insights for scientists studying other chalcogenide and pnictide superconductor materials. Additionally, our results highlight the capability of (Ba$_{0.6}$K$_{0.4}$)Fe$_{2}$As$_{2}$ to exhibit both conventional and unconventional superconducting phenomena depending on chemical composition. Moreover, our study reveals that this material exhibits a magnetic proximity effect due to anti-ferromagnetic order, which may be responsible for the opposition to superfluid flow observed in transport measurements. Two new strategies have emerged for applying the supersymmetry method to evaluate integrals involving bosonic and fermionic variables, specifically the superbosonization equation and the generalized Hubbard-Stratonovich transformation. We examine the fundamental connection between these strategies, demonstrating that the generalized Hubbard-Stratonovich transformation is a direct consequence of the superbosonization equation, and we also provide a straightforward transformation method for converting representations that employ the generalized Hubbard-Stratonovich transformation back to the standard supersymmetric format. Moreover, we introduce a novel'supersymmetric degree' metric to quantitatively assess the complexity of these transformation strategies. This metric not only facilitates comparison of the superbosonization equation and the generalized Hubbard-Stratonovich transformation but also enables generalization to more comprehensive transformations, such as the extended Hubbard-Stratonovich transformation, which we show possesses a higher supersymmetric degree than its predecessors. Additionally, we investigate how the complexity of these transformations is linked to the characteristics of the trial wavefunctions used in many-body quantum physics calculations. We contend that employing transformation strategies with higher supersymmetric degrees can yield more precise results, and we anticipate that this expectation will be substantiated by upcoming numerical simulations of ab initio quantum field theory simulations. Furthermore, we anticipate that the proposed'supersymmetric degree' metric will be valuable in exploring the intricate relationships between trial wavefunctions, transformation strategies, and simulation results in the context of ab initio quantum field theory simulations. Lastly, we introduce the term'supersymmetric degree' to capture the fundamental idea underlying these transformation strategies and suggest that it represents a crucial aspect of simulating supersymmetric field theories through ab initio quantum field theory simulations. Additionally, we note that the proposed'supersymmetric degree' metric is directly applicable to a broader class of transformations that derive their essence from the superbosonization equation and the generalized Hubbard-Stratonovich transformation. We anticipate that this concept will continue to yield important insights in the pursuit of optimal trial wavefunctions and transformation strategies for evaluating the path integral in quantum field theories. We anticipate that future studies using the proposed'supersymmetric degree' metric, combined with the degree of a trial wavefunction and the degree of a transformation strategy, will provide a comprehensive understanding of the complex relationships between these variables and simulation results in the context of ab initio quantum field theory simulations. We note that the term'supersymmetric degree' has been used to describe the fundamental idea underlying the superbosonization equation and the generalized Hubbard-Stratonovich transformation.

Initial findings from a measurement of the top quark's spin asymmetry, which would indicate its polarization, have been reported. The data, derived from 7 and 8 TeV proton-proton collisions respectively, totaled 4.7 inverse femtobarns of luminosity, were analyzed by searching for events featuring a W and a jet in their final states. The results showed a spin asymmetry value of 0.026, with a 95% confidence interval ranging from -0.044 to -0.008. This finding is relevant in validating theoretical models of the standard model, such as electroweak unification. These results demonstrate that the slow-recovering component is resistant to changes in LaNiO$_3$ layer thickness, while the fast-recovering component is significantly affected, displaying an opposing temperature dependence in thinner samples. Our study proposes a mathematical approach to pinpoint the origin of these photons, utilizing statistical patterns in the energies and arrival directions of photons above $10^{19}$ eV. The method quantifies the isotropic component of photon flux and its connection to the solar magnetic field's intensity. Our analysis of data from cosmic rays experiments AKARI, ASAS-SN, MAGIC, and VERITAS indicates that the effective photon flux above $10^{19}$ eV is less than $4.6\times 10^{-18}$ cm$^{-2}$s$^{-1}$, with an 95% confidence level. Additionally, our study finds that the solar magnetic field's intensity, as observed on Earth, is correlated with the siderial day of the solar cycle, exhibiting a seasonal variation linked to the solstice and equinox periods. The model predicts a functional relationship between the isotropic photon flux and the maximum solar flux, with a magnitude of variation of $1.9\times 10^{-3}$. Our research also reveals that photons above $10^{19}$ eV exhibit a energy dependence on their arrival directions, with an apparent slope of $0.38\pm 0.19$. Furthermore, we find that photons with energies above $10^{19}$ eV follow a power law distribution with a slope of $1.08\pm 0.21$, when corrected for the solar magnetic field's influence. Our study presents a new perspective on the nature of ultra-high energy photons and their relationship with the solar magnetic field, offering a theoretical framework that may be tested with upcoming multi-TeV cosmic rays experiments. Our results may also imply a connection between cosmic photons and solarpulsars, a previously undiscovered class of celestial objects proposed in an alternate solution to the missing baryon problem. Our study suggests that solarpulsars, which are inherently connected to the solar magnetic field's variability, may be the source of ultra-high energy photons observed on Earth. Distributed storage systems rely on replication to enhance both performance and reliability, but ensuring low latency data access requires handling updates without prior coordination. Asynchronous updates inevitably lead to conflict resolution issues with concurrent changes. A specific technique addressing this challenge is the "last-writer-wins" approach, which eliminates conflicts by overriding earlier updates, though it restricts performance benefits in concurrent reads. Our focus shifts to designs that allow for concurrent reads and explicit conflict resolution, providing a framework for creating replication systems using two main components: an update rule and a value space. We introduce a set of fundamental concepts, including "values," "operations," "values spaces," "update rules," and "sessions," and establish a theorem to guarantee conflict-free behavior. Additionally, we apply our framework to develop a few well-known replication systems, such as last-writer-wins, single-value replication, and distributed counters, as well as more complex systems like multi-key counters and set replication with last-writer-wins. Our approach is particularly useful for (1) educating students about the fundamental principles of replication, (2) providing a design framework for creating replication systems, and (3) validating the expressiveness of programming languages that support concurrent data types. To further refine the map, we performed in-depth analyses of seven traits, including discovery and validation of over 18,000 functional genomics regions and over 280 million association studies hits. Over time, the majority of these seemingly unrelated association studies hits (about 40%) gained functional relevance in later follow-up analyses, often due to an expansion of the functional genomics map as new evidence emerged or a redefinition of the underlying biology of the trait. The time it took for these initially unrelated association studies hits to become related varied greatly, from a few years to more than a decade, highlighting the dynamic nature of the map and the need for continuous refinement as new data becomes available. When we compared the functional genomics maps of different related traits, we found both a significant overlap in the underlying genetic variants and a significant variation in the specific functional genomics elements involved, which could be informed by the unique biological features of the underlying tissues used in the studies or the specific study designs employed. Furthermore, we developed an interactive web tool that enables users to explore the comprehensive functional genomics map, and this map is now an open resource available for public use. Additionally, we provided clear guidelines on the practical use of this map to interpret genome-wide association studies findings, including a new approach to prioritizing functional genomics regions based on their relevance to the underlying biology of a trait. This method, which takes advantage of the detailed information available in the map, includes a score that sums the level of confidence in the functional genomics region, the presence of associated studies hits within the underlying genetic variants, and the relevance of the specific functional genomics elements involved. This method offers a transparent and straightforward way to evaluate and compare the functional genomics maps of different genome-wide association studies, including those of large consortia. This approach to interpreting genome-wide association studies findings is highly extensible and is already being used to integrate new data into the map.

This paper discusses the underlying principles of the Minor Higgs System, a part of the Higgs boson detection infrastructure within the ATLAS experiment at the Large Hadron Collider. Despite being a secondary system, it plays a crucial role in validating the Higgs boson's properties and identifying potential beyond-Standard Model signatures, particularly in low-multiplicity final states involving the Higgs boson and a single or pair of top quarks. As the ATLAS experiment's primary goal is to characterize the Higgs boson's fundamental properties, the Minor Higgs System is essential for achieving this objective. It is also an important resource for further research at the Large Hadron Collider, and its capabilities will be reviewed in this paper, along with an overview of the methods and techniques used by ATLAS in identifying the Higgs boson in various contexts. Furthermore, this paper will cover outstanding theoretical predictions related to top-quark pair production and the search for the Standard Model's top-flavor equivalent of the Majoron, a dimensionless scalar that could address electroweak symmetry-breaking problems. In addition to these topics, this paper will also explore prospects for future research at the Large Hadron Collider. Observations of some variable X-ray sources within the Milky Way's center that have shown no outbursts in over a decade have led some researchers to suggest a significant population of stellar mass black holes in the region. A crucial aspect of the theory that there are no black holes is studying the recurrence times of neutron star binary systems that exhibit outbursts. By examining a comprehensive database of neutron star low-mass binary X-ray transient sources, researchers have found that the distribution of recurrence times is significantly shorter than a decade in nearly all systems. This insight has prompted a question about the status of quiescent X-ray binaries in the Milky Way, with outbursts that have not been observed recently. Ultimately, the fact that there are many such systems with short recurrence times and outbursts that have not been observed in over a decade supports the theory that these binaries are composed of neutron stars rather than stellar mass black holes. This conclusion is further validated by modeling the distribution of recurrence times using a population of active neutron star binaries, which closely matches the observed data. Additionally, this model indicates that about 80% of the putative neutron star binaries in the Milky Way exhibit outbursts from radio-luminous systems within 10 kiloparsecs of the Earth. This model also provides a method for detecting active neutron star binaries using a criterion based on the distribution of recurrence times, which has implications for the problem of hidden neutron star binaries. Furthermore, this approach to identifying active neutron star binaries is applicable to any population of binaries being observed with wide field-of-view X-ray telescopes. This research has highlighted the value of studying neutron star binary systems with outbursts and has underscored the importance of continued monitoring of the Galactic center and other nearby globular clusters with X-ray satellites that provide wide field-of-view observations. This strategy is not only crucial for resolving the nature of quiescent X-ray binaries in the Milky Way but also has a broader significance for the field of compact binary astrophysics. This knowledge has relevance to a wider range of phenomena, from the formation of neutron star and black hole binaries in the Milky Way to the formation of binary coalescence gravitational wave sources in the Milky Way and other galaxies. This research has also demonstrated that a key aspect of this broader range of phenomena can be addressed by studying the distribution of recurrence times of neutron star binary systems that exhibit outbursts. This understanding has been made possible by combining data from various X-ray satellites that have monitored the Galactic center and other nearby globular clusters over several decades

The breakdown of Newtonian physics at high acceleration and extreme mass ratio environments makes binary systems particularly sensitive to gravitational forces.  Due to their large separation, wide binary systems offer an alternative for studying gravity's impact, as their slow convergence allows for long-term observation of these systems.  Without a need for binary dynamics models, the velocity distribution in wide binaries follows a random orientation relative to the plane of the binary system, thus providing a straightforward test of general relativity's predictions.  Based on the velocity characteristics of wide binaries discovered by the Sloan Giant Segmented Array, we found that about 20% of these binaries conform to general relativity's predictions, with the remaining 80% showing a margin of $2\sigma$ deviation from the expected velocity distribution.  Without accounting for intermediate objects affecting the velocity distribution, we discovered that wide binaries located far from the Galactic plane are more likely to pass the test of gravity's validity, although the reason for this remains unclear.  Additionally, we found that wide binaries with greater angular sizes are more likely to fail the test, but this could be related to the detection bias associated with these systems.  Using models of the Milky Way, we mapped potential zones of strong gravitational forces affecting the velocity distribution of wide binaries, and we found that about 30% of these systems pass the test of gravity's validity in regions far from the Galactic center.  However, in regions close to the center where stars are densest, the failure rate rises to almost 90%.  Further study is needed to understand the implications of these findings for general relativity's theory.  Primary data analyzed in this study are now publicly available at the DOI link provided in the references. Radio sources within galaxy disks hold secrets to understanding how radio goods are produced and vary with environment.  Despite radio sources being bright, their power and other characteristics can be difficult to determine due to being distant in low-brightness radio fields.  Providing initial findings from a radio source stacking study, we discover that radio sources with low signal-to-noise ratios contain information about radio source characteristics, particularly their full width at half maximum.  We found that radio sources with smaller angular dimensions (less than 10") have a higher power output (log P approximately 23.3) and a narrower profile (full width at half maximum approximately 6.3") when compared to larger radio sources (above 10").  Additionally, we found that radio sources with smaller angular dimensions are more likely to be oriented at a greater angle (more than 45 degrees) to our line of sight.  All results hold true after controlling for radio source size and orientation using a likelihood approach.  All results are also consistent with previous findings from host galaxy studies.  We found a high correlation between power output and full width at half maximum (R approximately 0.88), a ratio of power output to size (log P/size approximately 1.05), as well as a narrow average radio source profile (full width at half maximum approximately 4.3").  All results provide a basis for radio source population studies as well as studies of extremely faint radio sources.  We found that radio sources with a power output above 10^23.5 have a power density that is significantly higher than that of radio sources with a power output below 10^23.  We found a higher average radio source power output for radio sources oriented at a smaller angle (less than 45 degrees) (log P approximately 23.5) when compared to radio sources oriented at a greater angle (more than 45 degrees) (log P approximately 23.1).  We found a higher average radio source full width at half maximum for radio sources oriented at a greater angle (more than 45 degrees) (approximately 5.6") when compared to radio sources oriented at a smaller angle (less than 45 degrees) (approximately 5.2").  We found a higher average radio source major to minor axis ratio for radio sources oriented at a greater angle (more than 45 degrees) (approximately 3.3) when compared to radio sources oriented at a smaller angle (less than 45 degrees) (approximately 2.5). We examine fast-moving fronts that form during massive star explosions and travel at over 1000 km/s through 10,000 km deep in the star's atmosphere. Using both numerical modeling and semi-analytical methods, we find that these high velocities can't be maintained throughout the entire depth of the atmosphere due to the increasing resistance from the stellar material. As a result, the shocks within 100-1000 km of the surface may become stationary and only begin moving at full velocity once this layer is overcome. Our models also show that the shocks can heat the star's atmosphere to incredibly high temperatures of up to 10^8 Kelvin, potentially creating massive amounts of electron-positron pairs that would significantly reduce the shocks' ability to emit x-ray and gamma-ray energy. Furthermore, our findings suggest that the pairs would only temporarily slow the shocks, allowing them to catch up and be re-accelerated as the front moves deeper into the star. This could result in the formation of extremely powerful and long-lasting blastwaves that could impact the surrounding interstellar medium. We validate our results using recent simulations of a massive star explosion and provide an initial condition model that other researchers can utilize for even more complex simulations involving multiple star explosions and interactions with the star's magnetic field. Additionally, we explore ways to observationally identify these shocks and the electron-positron pairs they create through the emission of x-rays and gamma-rays. Our model can help explain the recently observed relationships between the energy released in these explosions and the formation of black holes, as well as the phenomenon of pair-killed shocks. We also suggest that our model could be applicable to other types of explosions and rapid changes in massive stars and can be used to develop even more sophisticated simulations of these events. Our simulations demonstrate that even when the shocks become stationary, the front can still catch up as the star's material is slowly pushed out of the way, allowing the shocks to be re-accelerated and creating extremely powerful and long-lasting blastwaves that could impact the surrounding interstellar medium. We investigate the instantaneous electronic response to mechanical vibrations in a diamond cell containing nickel-doped gallium arsenide. Our results show significant changes in the spin splitting of conduction electrons when exposed to high hydrostatic pressure, a phenomenon that is not observed under uniaxial stress. The unusual behavior caused by mechanical stress at the material's band edges may lead to an increase in the spin splitting energy beyond what can be achieved through changes in composition or temperature. Notably, the band edge modifications occur only when the mechanical stress is anisotropic, resulting in a dependence on the orientation of the stress tensor. This unique phenomenon could potentially be harnessed for advanced optical spectroscopy or used to investigate the interactions between electrons, lattice vibrations, and the material's external environment. A method is proposed to utilize the described mechanical stress conditions for optical excitation and subsequent observation of the changes in the material's electronic structure. This approach could provide valuable insights into the fundamental properties of III-V semiconductors. Additionally, the proposed method may facilitate a direct connection between electrical and optical measurements of the materials' band edge modifications. A semiempirical model is presented to describe the behavior of diamond cell-contained materials and the resulting changes in the energy levels of the conduction band edge. A key factor influencing this behavior is the stress-induced change in the shape of the materials' Brillouin zone, a phenomenon that is unique to diamond cell-containing materials under mechanical stress. A significant increase in the spin splitting energy in diamond cell-contained materials may enable the utilization of these materials in advanced technological applications that require high spin splitting energy levels. A theoretical model is developed to describe the behavior of the spin splitting energy in these materials, which depends on various parameters, including the composition of the materials, the stress conditions, and the temperature. A key factor influencing this behavior is the change in the shape of the materials' Brillouin zone caused by the mechanical stress. A significant increase in the spin splitting energy in these materials may enable their utilization in advanced technological applications that require high spin splitting energy levels. A key aspect of this behavior is the change in the shape of the materials' Brillouin zone caused by the mechanical stress. A critical composition threshold is identified at approximately 1.5% nickel doping in gallium arsenide, where the largest spin splitting energy is observed. However, this threshold may vary depending on the specific materials and stress conditions. A significant amount of research remains to be conducted to fully understand the intricate relationships between composition, stress conditions, and temperature in these materials

Recent advances in natural language inference tasks have largely relied on models that are highly similar in architecture. Yet, nearly all of these have focused on a single, central scenario, incorporating implicit semantic varieties. In contrast, our work explores multiple natural language inference scenarios to recognize the diverse semantics present. We create a new, comprehensive dataset that combines 12 distinct scenarios, encompassing 144 unique semantic mixes. Our experiments demonstrate that current state-of-the-art models exhibit significant performance disparities across different scenarios and exhibit unexpected challenges when applying them to unfamiliar semantic contexts. We introduce novel evaluation metrics that account for both inferential and non-inferential aspects, along with several key model improvements. Ultimately, our results indicate that these advances yield notable enhancements in both aspects, proving particularly beneficial for scenarios that have not been previously explored. Our comprehensive dataset is open for public access at https://github.com/CHUIJIAN/nli-dialog. In addition, our code based on Transformers is available at https://github.com/CHUIJIAN/nli-dialog/tree/v1.0. You can download our model weights at https://drive.google.

The occurrence of sustainable hydrogen burning in very low-mass stars might be impacted by rotation due to the addition of centrifugal force and potential break-up caused by rapid spinning. Computer simulations model rotating low-mass stars with the capability for sustained nuclear reactions, considering a range of rotation rates, rather than slow rotation alone. Using these simulations, we determined the boundaries within which stars could maintain nuclear energy through hydrogen burning. These boundaries varied based on angular momentum. However, above a certain threshold (approximately 8.85 x 10^48 erg s) the boundaries broke into two distinct branches, resulting from objects losing mass up to a point where they break apart due to rapid rotation. Models with less than this threshold were either stopped from further nuclear reactions by mass loss, or they broke apart and couldn't be modeled because of limitations in the computer simulations. Models with more than this threshold could complete nuclear energy through hydrogen burning, but only if their initial masses were less than 0.9 times the mass of the Sun. Converting these simulations into observations, we found that out of 20 simulated objects, detectable evidence of hydrogen burning in very low-mass stars through X-ray emission would be visible up to 10.8 billion years into the future. Additionally, potential artifacts in models that incorporate external angular momentum sources don't affect the overall limitations set by internal angular momentum on the hydrogen burning phase. Lastly, implementing these simulations into our understanding of the PSO J318.5-22, an object previously believed to be a failed star, suggests that its internal angular momentum is within the range necessary for it to be considered a low-mass brown dwarf with failed hydrogen burning in its core. However, if the origin of the object is linked to the disruption of a small star by a black hole, then its hydrogen burning capability could still be active. Finally, these simulations also reveal that objects like the PSO J318.5-22 will be typical of objects that fail hydrogen burning in very low-mass stars over a wide range of rotation rates. However, this analysis faces a major challenge in addressing instrumental influences 
such as fluctuations in background levels and selection efficiency across different 
multidimensional kinematic scenarios.  This article will review traditional methods 
used for treating instrumental variables and highlight the advantages of a more 
recent approach developed by Daum, which employs the detailed bin-by-bin method. 
This approach involves a clear interpretation of instrumental variables as quantities 
related to experimental results, which can be analyzed using maximum likelihood fits. 
The article will also discuss the application of this method to various analyses.

and provides a detailed explanation of the theoretical basis of the detailed bin-by- 
bin method in the context of amplitude analysis. The article is concluded by 
highlighting the recent progress made possible by this method, specifically in 
the case of $B^0$ decaying to either at least one photon or to a meson and a

Bipartite graphs depicting connections between distinct groups of objects have numerous practical applications, and their visualization often takes the form of a 2-tier layout where corresponding entities are aligned horizontally across two parallel lines, connected by lines representing relationships between them. The task of reducing edge crossings within these visualizations can be computationally intensive, yet might not always guarantee sufficiently low crossings to maintain the visualization's clarity. In contrast, an approach is presented that efficiently minimizes edge crossings while preventing any adjacent relationships from being placed on top of each other, effectively serving as a pre-processing step for subsequent layouts. Furthermore, this approach is proven to be computationally viable and includes a pseudo-polynomial algorithm for calculating the minimum number of crossings prior to routing relationships between entities. The proposed method is then applied to a real-world scenario involving election data, yielding a more manageable visualization than existing layouts. The provided code can be found on GitHub at the specified link. The approach is also adaptable to a variety of bipartite graph formats and might be explored for extension to general graph layouts. Feedback from both domain experts and graph visualization specialists has been incorporated into the approach, and their recommended modifications are discussed. The term "routing" is avoided in favor of "mapping" to better reflect the method's objectives and constraints. The approach is capable of handling instances with up to 5000 nodes, but its performance decreases for larger nodes in the graph. The approach is now referred to as BVS, short for Bipartite Vertex Splitting, and its components, such as simplified subgraphs and the REBUS algorithm, are discussed in more detail. The scope of BVS is defined as limited to bipartite graphs, and its effectiveness is compared to existing methods on a variety of datasets. The code for the REBUS algorithm is available on GitHub at the specified link. The time complexity of the reoptimization step is reduced from O(n^2) to O(n), and the resulting program is capable of handling instances with up to 7000 nodes. The method is still computationally intensive, and several potential improvements are discussed, such as employing different vertex splittings, eliminating the ordering constraint, and employing a more efficient data structure. The approach is applied to a real-world election dataset, and the resulting mappings are presented along with their corresponding crossings and areas. The potential applications of the approach are discussed, and several future research directions are outlined, including its extension to general graphs and the integration of additional constraints. Deep neural network approaches have achieved great success in various AI tasks, particularly in image recognition tasks. Deep neural network approaches leverage incremental learning techniques, allowing them to efficiently learn from growing datasets by gradually adding new classes. However, a significant challenge in this area arises when dealing with imbalanced class incremental learning scenarios, characterized by unbalanced data distribution changes. Existing research has primarily focused on addressing the baseline class incremental learning issue, leaving the underlying problem of dealing with data imbalance unresolved. In contrast, our work explores this related issue by investigating the use of widely adopted calibration methods to address the prediction bias exacerbation in ICIIL scenarios. We introduce a comprehensive evaluation protocol, encompassing both theoretical analysis and experimental validation. Our findings, revealed through the evaluation of six popular calibration methods on three diverse datasets, highlight the prevalence of prediction bias in the ICIIL context and its mitigating effectiveness via the use of reweighting, relabeling, and posterior calibration techniques. Our work offers a valuable contribution to the field by highlighting the significance of data imbalance issues in machine learning and the need for further research into the development of efficient algorithms capable of addressing this complex challenge. We have made our code publicly available for easy access via the following link: https://github.com/zwang84/ICIL-Calibration. We anticipate this work to facilitate engaging discussions on the data imbalance issue in the machine learning community and contribute to the ongoing pursuit of innovative solutions. Additionally, we have introduced an open-source code base that enables researchers to explore a wide range of calibration methods and context-aware strategies in the ICIL context. This versatile code framework, built using the PyTorch platform, may be adapted to accommodate various network architectures, data sources, and scenario specifications, making it an invaluable resource for the community. We believe this resource to not only benefit the machine learning community but also contribute to the growth of the PyTorch ecosystem. We have further extended this open-source code base to facilitate seamless experimentation with a diverse range of calibration methods in the ICIL context. As a result, the Higgs-induced correction to the muon's magnetic moment is more substantial than previously estimated, rising from a $0.002\sigma$ effect to $0.005\sigma$, and is now closer to resolving the discrepancy between the observed and theoretical values of the muon's magnetic moment. This improvement in the anomaly's size comes from a more accurate assessment of the Higgs mass correction, which is critical because the Higgs boson's mass is largely composed of the top quark's contribution, often overlooked in renormalization procedures. As the Higgs sector's involvement in electroweak precision is relatively minor, the improved estimate for this contribution suggests the Higgs' impact on the muon's magnetic moment could soon be sufficiently precise to distinguish it from beyond-the-Standard Model explanations. Furthermore, incorporating this updated calculation method will likely lead to a more significant contribution from the Higgs to the muon's electric dipole moment, making it more substantial than previously estimated and indicative of new physics at a high mass scale. As such, the Higgs' impact on the muon's magnetic and electric dipole moments should be more accurately represented in global fits of beyond-the-Standard Model scenarios. As the Higgs anomaly within the Standard Model model is already at the edge of statistical significance and expected to become more pronounced with more data, the revised calculation method used here highlights the importance of further investigating the Higgs' role in the anomaly. As such, we suggest the anomaly's origin could be a multi-faceted problem involving both the Higgs and the significant effect the top quark has on the muon's magnetic moment, which is a fundamental, expected phenomenon within the Standard Model. As expected, we also find that the previously reported discrepancy in the muon's magnetic moment is more significant when considering the Higgs and the top quark together. As the Higgs contributes substantially to the anomaly, models aiming to resolve the discrepancy by addressing the Standard Model's shortcomings should reconsider the Higgs' role, while models aiming to provide a solution by significantly impacting the muon's magnetic moment or making it anomalous should ensure their proposed solution applies broadly to both the magnetic moment and the electric dipole moment. In the context of the development of computational methods for approximating matrix functions, recent advancements in computational technology have prompted a reevaluation of traditional algorithms for optimal performance. By leveraging the exceptional capabilities of high-performance computers, matrix function estimation can now be achieved through divisible algorithms, taking full advantage of multiple processors. This involves decomposing numerical operations into smaller, independent steps that can be concurrently solved, resulting in significant speed gains. However, the complexity of matrix functions introduces an inherent barrier, as the development of divisible algorithms is complicated by the interdependence of matrix elements in certain operations. This paper explores the implementation of matrix multiplication using two methods: a sequential approach and a divisible approach. Our experiments, conducted using a single core central processing unit (CPU) and a graphics processing unit (GPU), reveal the substantial performance benefits of the divisible approach. Interestingly, our findings indicate that the CPU's ability to support very large matrix sizes makes it preferred for these applications, at least with the current technological limitations. Conversely, the GPU's ability to handle highly complex matrix operations exceeds that of the CPU. As a result, we are able to define problem parameters that optimize performance on each processor. As an illustrative example, our research demonstrates the potential applications of matrix multiplication in solving polynomial equations using the Muirhead and Cartan formulas. Additionally, our results highlight the scope for further optimization in the development of divisible algorithms. Furthermore, we are exploring the extension of our CPU-GPU framework to enable the solution of complex numerical problems involving matrix functions. This integrated approach aims to leverage the complementary strengths of these processors, leveraging the exceptional processing capabilities of the GPU while also utilizing the CPU's ability to support larger matrix sizes. This combined approach is expected to yield a more significant performance improvement resulting from the seamless collaboration of these processors. However, implementing this level of integration poses significant software development challenges. Therefore, our research is being undertaken in an environment of rapid technological change, where hardware advancements can often outpace software innovations, rendering it essential to acknowledge the methodological difficulties encountered in this study. Nonetheless, our results provide valuable insights into the performance evaluation of sequential and divisible algorithms. Moreover, our experience with the development of divisible algorithms for matrix multiplication has implications for the broader field of numerical analysis. This is because the advancement of computational technology is an ongoing process, where the constant improvement of processor technologies presents new opportunities and challenges for the development of numerical algorithms. This, in turn, has important implications for the research community, as the opportunity exists to explore a range of research questions arising from these developments.

As deep neural networks require massive amounts of high-quality data to achieve optimal performance, it's common for them to struggle with operational environments that are dynamic, multi-sensor basins, and include a variety of anomalies. In response, the models developed in such situations tend to be overfitting, unreliable, and prone to severe security vulnerabilities. To address this challenge, we propose a multi-agent system that combines machine learning learning and artificial intelligence. This system consists of two components: a machine learning model that is trained on a subset of high-quality data labeled by a user and a large amount of low-quality, unreliable data labeled as "invalid"; and an artificial intelligence module that generates a large amount of high-quality training data from a small set of reliable samples through data augmentation. The machine learning model classifies input data as "valid" or "invalid", while the artificial intelligence module creates a trust score for each sample based on its classification and the model's confidence.
