In this research, we propose a method to automatically generate complex road networks for testing the limits of autonomous lane-keeping technology in simulation. By using a set of control points to create a parametric road design, we define a driving task that an equipped vehicle must perform. Modifying the control points significantly impacts the road's overall shape and layout. Our approach leverages optimization techniques to identify a set of control points that creates challenging driving conditions, causing the vehicle to veer off its intended path. We validated our method with three distinct search configurations, focusing on balancing testing speed and practicality for simulated evaluations of autonomous lane-keeping systems. Our method shows promising results in replicating difficult driving experiences in a simulated environment, which is a crucial aspect for comprehensive system testing. Furthermore, our approach facilitates the efficient generation of diverse, high-quality test cases at a moderate computational cost. We made our method accessible through an open-source Python package called BeerNet, which is openly available on GitHub. By utilizing BeerNet, other researchers can develop their own search strategies to create customized road networks that mimic real-world scenarios. We included a preliminary analysis of the generated networks in our study, and future work is planned to further explore the integration of BeerNet with expertise-driven search methods. By doing so, we aim to create more sophisticated, realistic road networks that mimic the complexities found in actual urban environments. We anticipate this development to contribute positively to the advancement of testing tools for autonomous vehicle systems. We published a conference paper detailing our method and accompanying testing results at the 2023 IEEE Intelligent Transportation Systems Conference (ITSC). Our research is ongoing, and we are currently exploring ways to integrate our system with third-party tools and software used in the development of autonomous vehicles. One potential future project could involve collaborating with the Open Autonomous Systems Testbed (OAST) initiative, which focuses on creating open-source testing tools for autonomous systems. We are also open to receiving feedback and guidance from the broader research community in further developing our method and testing results. A recently investigated explanation suggests that these structures form when magnetic field eddies caused by edge-localized modes trigger the development of a PTM seed island. However, this study instead seeks to provide an alternate explanation based on observations of edge plasma turbulence. A distinct feature of plasma turbulence is the existence of persistent structures known as blobs and holes in the scrape-off-layer. We examine the potential of a proposed TeV-scale muon collider, studying the technical feasibility and scientific advantages of this type of collider. Considering existing R&D efforts and the progress made so far, we believe a muon collider with 1.5 TeV and 5-7 invograms of luminosity could be achieved by the mid-2030s. To assess the scientific value of such a collider, we evaluate its capability to drive future colliders, including a next-generation $e^+e^-$ collider and a 100 TeV proton collider, and find that it would be highly effective in doing so. Furthermore, we find that a muon collider would be substantially more efficient in discovering new physics than a 100 TeV hadron collider or a 1 TeV $e^+e^-$ collider built from converted components, with the potential to achieve a factor of five more sensitivity in certain areas. In addition to its scientific potential, we highlight several practical benefits of a muon collider, including its ability to directly discover a broad mass range of new physics, as well as its ability to serve as a model for future colliders. We discuss the requirements for achieving the required performance levels, including the need for multiple stages of gradient enhancement and the potential risks associated with beam training at high energy levels. We also consider the option of incorporating a conversion of an existing particle accelerator into a muon collider, which could potentially reduce the technical risk and the required development time. Finally, we outline the necessary R&D paths and the necessary milestones for achieving the required performance levels by the mid-2030s, including several areas where further theoretical and computational research is also needed. We conclude that a TeV-scale muon collider is a technically feasible and scientifically valuable proposition worth seriously considering for construction in the mid-2030s. We also highlight that the case for a muon collider is robust enough to be worthy of discussion with international collaborators and relevant stake-holders. We define "loom area" for a surface in a 3-dimensional space as the smallest possible projection area when the surface is projected perpendicularly onto a nearby plane. We then investigate how loom areas relate to veering triangulations, particularly focusing on surfaces generated by pseudo-Anosov flows. Building on an earlier observation by Bestvina and Kaimanovich, we discovered that in a veering triangulation, loom areas are all equal to the base angle squared, which is pi squared in the case of ideal hyperbolic space. We also found a different proof of this fact by comparing loom areas to angles within veering triangulations. Furthermore, we established that a veering triangulation can be determined by its loom areas, providing a new characterization. Additionally, we explored how loom areas change along rays in veering triangulations, discovering that this behavior creates a non-decreasing sequence that ultimately reaches a limit equal to the square of an irrational number, which can also be thought of as the square of the length of a perpendicular line segment in a specific situation. This research also enables us to offer a precise description of how loom areas increase in a manner reflected in the geometry of veering triangulations. We utilized both geometric and combinatorial approaches in our investigations. We also found connections between our results and aspects of leaf space geometry, combinatorics within veering triangulations, and the behavior of rays in these structures. Finally, we established that in a particular type of veering triangulation based on a rational flow, loom areas will all be rational numbers. We used both our new findings and existing knowledge about veering triangulations to prove this fact. On the other hand, given a set of equal loom areas in a 3-dimensional space, we can apply Milnor's technique to create a singular surface. We then investigate the type of singularities that can arise under different circumstances. We also used our new results to show that in a particular type of veering triangulation based on a rational flow, the surface will have singularities with very low indices. Building on this, we proved that in a situation where the surface has a particular type of boundary, the veering triangulation can be constructed using only combinatorial methods. We utilized both our new findings and existing knowledge about veering triangulations to prove this fact. Graph neural networks have excelled in multiple applications by leveraging graph representation learning. These models combine node features with the graph structure, creating powerful and interpretable models. To prevent overfitting and reduce computational costs, model practitioners often employ sparse versions of graph neural networks by selectively retaining a limited number of important edges. The process of edge selection, however, is typically achieved through randomized methods or unsophisticated techniques that don't consider the underlying characteristics of the graph or the models used for prediction. We introduce an innovative approach called Learned Sparsification, which involves training a student model that selectively ignores parts of the graph data by mapping the original graph signals to a reduced representation. By doing so, we leverage optimization techniques to determine the most crucial graph edges that produce a highly accurate and interpretable model. Compared to existing methods, our approach results in a significant improvement in classification accuracy, as evidenced by our experiments on publicly available datasets obtained from the PyTorch-Geometric repository. Notably, our method achieved a notable 0.4% improvement in accuracy on the PubMed dataset, 0.6% improvement on the PubMed-Citation dataset, and 1.5% improvement on the PPI dataset. Furthermore, our approach offers a more sustainable alternative to the current state-of-the-art models. In collaboration with domain experts, we demonstrated that our learned sparsification framework can identify hidden patterns in the data and produce a more compact and accurate model. For instance, on the Cora dataset, our model identified a key subgroup of authors with a high citation rate, thereby highlighting the interpretability benefits of our approach. Additionally, our results show that our method can mitigate the impact of noisy edge attachments on the model's performance, as shown in experiments conducted on publicly available datasets obtained from the PyTorch-Geometric repository. Effective management of controllable loads relies on the strategic deployment of aggregators that can efficiently convey their flexible capabilities, referred to as aggregate flexibility, to system operators. Current approaches typically involve time-consuming estimates, with minimal focus on real-time coordination between aggregators and operators. This paper proposes a solution to an online optimization problem within a closed-loop system by introducing a real-time feedback mechanism known as maximum entropy feedback (MEF). Analytical properties of MEF are examined, and it is shown that MEF can be approximated through reinforcement learning and utilized as a penalty term in the penalized predictive control (PPC) algorithm, an adaptation of model predictive control (MPC). Key benefits of our approach include (1) reduced communication demands for operators, requiring only MEF information, (2) faster computational processing due to lower variable counts, and (3) lower operational costs, with certain assumptions indicating optimal performance. The proposed PPC is evaluated on an adaptive electric vehicle charging dataset, yielding superior outcomes compared to traditional MPC methods. Moreover, our approach is currently integrated into the Google XG portfolio management platform, providing real-world evidence of its practical applicability. We introduce SCATTER, a novel theoretical framework that generates universal envelope theorems applicable to various abstract data structures used for searching and sorting. These theorems provide a comprehensive proof of at least one order of magnitude better performance compared to brute force methods. We demonstrate the validity of SCATTER by creating specific envelope theorems tailored to ordered arrays, linked lists, and search trees, which all yield sublinear or linear performance benefits. Furthermore, we show that many established results in computer science, including certain algorithms and problem reductions, naturally adhere to the SCATTER framework, thereby guaranteeing their optimal performance. We also establish a crucial property that any two distinct elements within a given structure can be compared in constant time. Building upon this foundation, we develop various envelope theorems that can compare multiple elements with the same constant time complexity, regardless of the underlying data structure. Ultimately, we conclude that any data structure supporting comparison of elements is equivalent to having access to a form of sorting, which is capable of sorting a subarray of length k in linear time. We then leverage this equivalence to derive even more efficient algorithms for a wide range of problems, incorporating both online and offline components, which can be solved in near-optimal time using our proposed methods. We also address certain hardness levels, such as those involving large subsets and elements with distinct values, and find that these conditions can be overcome with our technique of using a smaller subset of elements. We apply our method to various optimization problems, including resource allocation, activity selection, and minimum spanning trees, and successfully solve a wide range of minimum sum problems with multiple elements. We showcase our method's effectiveness on real-world datasets, achieving a significant performance improvement of at least an order of magnitude better than the baseline performance. We also provide a comprehensive analysis of our approach using various metrics, including running time, memory usage, and solution quality, and find that our method outperforms the baseline in all these aspects. We conclude by highlighting the broad applicability of our approach and its potential to be applied to a wide range of problems in computer science. We also provide a comprehensive overview of our method, including a step-by-step description of how we applied the SCATTER framework to solve the given problems. We believe that our approach will be beneficial for any student who is trying to solve problems using algorithm design techniques and data structures. We hope that by presenting our solution in a transparent and step-by-step manner, we can provide valuable insights to both students and experts in the field of computer science. This research investigates double Higgs boson production at future electron-positron colliders CLIC and ILC with TeV-scale energies within the framework of Effective Field Theories, with a focus on the Higgs sector's beyond-Standard Model contributions. We examine the valid range of scales up to several TeV and consider four effective operators affecting Higgs interactions: a top-quark contact, a bottom-quark contact, a Higgs self-interaction, and a dark Higgs portal. Our study shows that the double Higgs production process is the most sensitive to the top-quark contact operator, with CLIC operating at 3 TeV providing the best results, with effective new physics scales as low as 1 TeV-10 TeV potentially detectable in the order of 10 femtobarn inverse energy units. We find that ILC with a center-of-mass energy of 1 TeV can achieve comparable or better sensitivities than CLIC at lower energy scales, and that the sensitivity to the top-quark contact operator depends on both the operator's coefficient and relevant dimensionless pre-factor, demonstrating the significance of thorough theoretical predictions in the interpretation of experimental data. Additionally, we find that the expected performance of optimized searches for double Higgs production, covered in our analysis, mirrors that of current limits from LHC Run 2. Our study also highlights that future electron-positron colliders have significant discovery potential for double Higgs production across a wide range of effective operator coefficients, with potential for significant improvements in sensitivity with optimized searches in relation to thorough theoretical predictions. Our research paves the way for a comprehensive investigation of other beyond-Standard Model scenarios in the Higgs sector at future electron-positron colliders. Our study has been shared with the ILC and CLIC working groups and contributes to the ongoing discussion to optimize the search for double Higgs production at these colliders. Our analysis code is publicly available online. We investigated the motion of a cylindrical object moving within a plane parallel to its major and minor axes across the surface of a granular material partially saturated with a liquid, and the effects it has on the object's behavior. By examining how the object's shape affects its movement, we discovered that its motion is influenced by a anisotropic force that opposes its movement, and that this anisotropic force is caused by the object's interaction with the granular material. This results in the object experiencing a greater resistance when moving perpendicular to its major axes than when moving parallel to its minor axes. This phenomenon of anisotropic drag can be explained by the object's tendency to get stuck in the granular material at its narrow end, and we demonstrated that this behavior leads to the object's movement in a curved path when pushed in a straight line. This phenomenon of anisotropic drag may be relevant to the movement of cylindrical objects such as balls in similar environments. Additionally, we found that the object's movement could be influenced by surface tension and the viscosity of the surrounding liquid, and that these factors caused the object to experience an additional force that pushed it in a direction away from the point where the liquid was in contact with the granular material and the object. However, the factors to which the object is subject include not just its motion but also how its motion affects the surrounding liquid and the object itself. This means that the object's motion is part of a more complex system that includes how its motion affects the liquid and the object, and how they in turn affect the object's motion. Using observations from KCWI and NOEMA, we studied a distant starburst galaxy, examining how star formation-driven gas outflows are linked to other properties of the galaxy. Our data show a significant outflow in the central region of the galaxy, powered by massive star formation. In contrast, ionized gas outflows are minimal in regions far from the center. We found that the rate of star formation decreases with greater distance from the galaxy's center, while the mass of gas and the outflow velocity remain relatively constant across different regions. Our results imply that the control of outflows exerts a damping effect on the conversion of gas to stars, thereby limiting the formation of stars in regions far from the galaxy's center. Moreover, we found that the relationship between the mass of gas and the outflow velocity can be explained by an equation that relates these factors to the energy generated by star formation and the ways in which gas is expelled from the galaxy. This relationship enables us to determine the energy required to generate outflows and the efficiency with which this energy is utilized. We found this energy to be $10^{38}$ dyne-cm/s^2, a value that, when coupled with outflow velocities observed in other galaxies, implies a universal energy scaling of $L_\mathrm{outflow} \propto L_\mathrm{UV}^{1.12}$. This study combines radio and optical observations to gain a deeper understanding of the link between star formation, gas outflows, and galaxy evolution. It showcases the capabilities of new radio and optical telescopes that allow for the simultaneous observation of gas and star light in galaxies across the universe. Observations of the interaction between star formation and gas outflows in galaxies will provide critical insights into the processes that govern the evolution of galaxies. Furthermore, we propose a new method to measure the effectiveness with which energy from star formation is utilized to drive gas outflows and promote the conversion of gas to stars. This method can be applied to a vast number of galaxies observed with radio and optical telescopes that allow for the simultaneous observation of gas and star light in galaxies across the universe. In the context of a large study on 50 galaxies observed with KCWI and NOEMA, we found that the control of outflows exerts a damping effect on the conversion of gas to stars, resulting in a relationship that could lead to a better understanding of the link between star formation, gas outflows, and galaxy evolution. Additionally, we discovered that the velocity of outflows remains relatively constant with greater distance from the galaxy

Current auto-tuning frameworks for computer systems face challenges due to their large configuration spaces and the difficulties associated with evaluating their performance. Recently, our research team developed an innovative approach called BoGraph, an organized Bayesian optimization method that leverages system logs to speed up the tuning process. By combining performance data with configuration relationships, BoGraph creates an interactive graph that guides its optimization process. This technique surpasses state-of-the-art methods, according to our experiments, and we believe our results, particularly our demonstration of BoGraph's performance on a real-world application, can inspire others to explore similar approaches. Additionally, our code is now publicly available to facilitate further development and improvement. BayesOpt previously led the pack in auto-tuning computer systems due to its exceptional performance, however our new approach not only outperforms BayesOpt but also sheds light on a crucial aspect often overlooked in BayesOpt applications, namely the importance of system knowledge. This new insight, combined with the fact that our approach outperforms BayesOpt on every benchmark, has significant implications for the broader BayesOpt community. Our method's results show a notable increase in performance, amounting to up to 5 times better results in some cases. This gain is attributed to two key factors: the reduction of unnecessary evaluations, achieved by exploiting the organizational structure of the configuration, as well as the ability to effectively handle a wide range of expensive systems with many parameters. This is further highlighted by our analysis of the underlying economics of these optimization tasks, revealing a connection between our approach and the famous Baker's Dozen. Although our method's performance surpasses all current auto-tuning methods, there is still room for improvement, especially in cases where the system exhibits a high degree of irregularity. Our research also sheds light on an interesting phenomenon, where the combination of a good BayesOpt implementation and a thorough understanding of the system under evaluation can result in a level of performance that approaches the theoretical maximum achievable with a given configuration. This is a key lesson that our results demonstrate through three distinct perspectives. Our approach is an auto-tuning method that not only outperforms all current techniques, but it also provides valuable insights that can be applied to other BayesOpt applications. Additionally, our work raises an interesting question about the optimal number of parameters that a system should have, and our results suggest that future research should focus on systems with at least 5-7 key parameters. Our research examined the connection between initial anisotropic geometry and anisotropic flow within a multiphase transport model, specifically for 200 GeV Au+Au and Cu+Cu collisions. Contrary to elliptical flow's dependence on centrality, we discovered minimal variation in initial anisotropic geometry with increasing centrality. However, triangular flow's centrality dependence mirrors that of elliptical flow. Once the influence of initial anisotropic geometry is removed through ratio calculations, differences in initial state and flow behavior become apparent, exhibiting varying responses to increasing centrality across Au+Au and Cu+Cu collisions. Additionally, we found that the initial anisotropic radius and flow velocity exhibit distinct relationships depending on transverse momentum. A separate investigation into the initial anisotropic radius's components revealed the influence of nucleon-size corrections on initial anisotropic geometry. Nucleon-size corrections' effect on triangular flow varies with transverse momentum and centrality. Furthermore, this model predicts that the initial anisotropic radius's ratio in Cu+Cu collisions will be greater than in Au+Au collisions of the same centrality, resulting in increased triangular flow in corresponding midrapidity bins. Over the years, the availability of Linked Data has surged exponentially with more than 10,000 online datasets now available and formatted according to Linked Data standards, enabling seamless machine readability and interconnectivity.  While such datasets provide numerous opportunities, numerous applications remain hindered due to data of poor quality, significantly affecting tasks such as data integration, search, and interlinking.  Existing quality assessment techniques for Linked Data, although limited, suffer from decreased effectiveness with rising data sizes and become unmanageable for single-machine operations.  To address these challenges, our proposed DistQualityFramework is an open-source, cluster-enabled implementation designed for comprehensive quality evaluation of large-scale RDF datasets, leveraging the processing capabilities of Apache Spark to distribute quality metrics computation.  This innovative, distributed in-memory approach allows for flexible metric extension via a provided quality assessment pattern and, through seamless integration with the SANSA framework, also enables efficient Semantic Mapping Applications.  The proposed framework exhibits superior performance compared to existing methodologies, as demonstrated by its application to large-scale datasets containing up to 3 billion triples.  Furthermore, DistQualityFramework is made available for the research community to further develop its scalable and efficient design. This innovative, distributed approach constitutes a significant step forward in the effective evaluation of large-scale Linked Data sets. By applying a direct method to solve the optimization problem, we significantly reduce the computational complexity from exponential growth to O(N^3), where N represents the number of data points. Furthermore, our approach facilitates explicit expression of the estimated parameters in terms of the data and specified functional forms, enabling a more intuitive understanding of their behavior. To illustrate the effectiveness of this method, we conduct a simulation study comparing our approach to conventional maximum likelihood estimation, revealing a notable improvement in efficiency. Additionally, we apply this method to analyze real-world data from wheat yield experiments, obtaining a comprehensive analysis of the interactions between environmental factors and the time course of wheat growth. The proposed estimation approach is adaptable to a broad class of regression models, including non-linear models and models with distributed parameters, and is publicly available for public use through an R package. Edge computing delivers faster processing times and lower latency for applications by moving processing closer to user locations.  Despite this, researching scenarios and evaluating edge systems can be complicated due to various factors such as multiple system configurations, differing data sets, and varied application needs.  Existing evaluation methods are often inflexible and don't account for changes throughout the process, which is where traditional evaluation frameworks fall short.  To address these limitations, we propose a revolutionary new approach called EDE, an event-driven evaluation method for edge platforms.  EDE is an open-source tool that allows for flexible, dynamic evaluation of edge systems, user locations, system configurations, data sets, and application functions, even in scenarios with changing conditions.  In experiments using a scenario with varying loads and a real-world traffic monitoring scenario, EDE demonstrated significant advantages over other evaluation methods, revealing a 5x to 10x performance difference in edge system evaluations.  The EDE project is currently hosted on GitHub at https://github.com/edgeai-org/edge-ai.org/tree/main/examples/ede.  The detailed evaluation results are available at https://edgeai.org/evaluations.  Edge AI has incorporated the EDE framework into its benchmark suite available at https://edgeai.org/benchmarks.  To use the EDE framework for other applications, a tutorial on using EDE is available at https://edgeai.org/tutorials/edge-deep-learning-benchmarking.  The study reveals that EDE's flexible, data-independent approach is well-suited for complex, real-world scenarios and significantly outperforms other evaluation methods.  Furthermore, the results show that current edge models often struggle with real-world data sets, which underscores the need for more robust evaluation methods and greater realism in benchmarking edge AI systems.  Ultimately, the future of edge AI depends on its ability to efficiently process real-time video streams with varying conditions, such as those encountered in high-way surveillance.  On this note, the edge community should adopt and extend the EDE framework to develop more effective evaluation methods.  Additionally, the study highlights the significance of collaborating with practitioners in refining evaluation methods and benchmark suites to ensure they accurately reflect real-world scenarios.  The edge computing field requires a more flexible and dynamic approach to evaluation methods that can handle diverse system configurations, data sets, and application functions.  The EDE project is a significant step in this direction by developing a flexible, event-driven evaluation method for edge platforms.  The study's findings also emphasize the need for more robust edge models

To address this challenge, we propose SceneGen, a cutting-edge traffic scenario generation system based on advanced neural network techniques. SceneGen starts with a detailed description of the environment and participant information, which serves as input. It then utilizes a multi-stage approach, combining text-to-image models and 3D rendering, to create highly detailed and visually accurate traffic scenes. To ensure SceneGen produces realistic outcomes, we've developed several post-processing methods, which include participant position adjustment and scene path feasibility checking. When evaluated using existing traffic scenario datasets, SceneGen demonstrated its capacity for creating diverse, realistic scenarios. Additionally, SceneGen was found to be data-efficient, producing a large dataset consisting of 5000 detailed traffic scenes with minimal starting data. The code and models for SceneGen have been made publicly available. To further advance the field, we also introduce MIST, a comprehensive benchmark focused on evaluating 3D traffic scenario understanding and generation. This comprehensive benchmark assesses various aspects, including participant classification, scene recognition, and overall scene creation. The results from evaluating SceneGen against MIST's diverse metrics have shown its strength compared to other competing approaches. When implemented in an end-to-end simulation environment, SceneGen-derived scenarios resulted in accurate prediction of real-world lane change behaviors. Consequently, SceneGen has the potential to significantly contribute to the development of realistic traffic scenario datasets and models required by advanced vehicle simulation systems. Moreover, its comprehensive benchmark, MIST, will likely become a leading standard for evaluating and comparing traffic scenario generation methods. The models consist of a 20 solar mass molecular cocoon surrounded by a 10 solar mass circumstellar envelope, with metal content set at zero. Using a sophisticated radiation transport module, we simulated the star's interaction with its surroundings, accounting for radiative acceleration, electron exhaust ionization, and dust particle growth. Our models demonstrated significant dust growth, resulting from the interaction between the hot inner layer of the cocoon and a 10 kilometer thick dust layer within the star's outer layer. This dust growth occurs when a significant amount of electron-exhaust layers are pushed back into the cool cocoon by expanding gas, causing the formation of a 10 astronomical unit large interface between the inner layer and the cooler cocoon. As a result of this interface, a significant amount of dust is formed within a few astronomical units of the interface, displaying a 10 kilometer radius. Due to the influence of radiative acceleration, a significant amount of gas is ejected into the surrounding interstellar medium in the form of globules, dust particles, and small particles at high velocities, exceeding the sound speed. Additionally, a significant amount of gas is released into the interstellar medium by an expanding thin shell and a large amount of dust particles released by globules. Detecting and classifying objects in three-dimensional space has significant implications for areas like navigation, robotics, and self-driving technology. Despite advancements in 2D object detection, there remains a significant gap in 3D object identification due to the scarcity and unbalanced distribution of 3D annotations in training datasets. This disparity becomes especially pronounced in distant or overlapping objects, where even minor discrepancies in measurement readings can result in significantly different 3D coordinates. This problem was initially introduced by Liu et al. in 3D Center Format (3DF) annotation, which standardizes center coordinates, radius, and orientation for 3D objects. To address this challenge, our model Far3Det learns 3DF information from scratch, using two separate 2D detectors for x and y coordinates and a single 2D classifier for 3DF attributes. This approach allows Far3Det to efficiently identify 3D objects in real-time while minimizing the requirement for 3DF annotations. Far3Det has been successfully applied to various evaluation benchmarks, achieving exceptional performance on real-world datasets while exhibiting a substantial reduction in annotation costs. This paper presents Far3Det, a pioneering approach that has been made open-source for the benefit of the research community. We have incorporated Far3Det into the Detectron2 framework, and it is available on GitHub under the Apache-2.0 license. Through extensive experiments and analyses, we have demonstrated Far3Det's efficacy, efficiency, and safety for 3D object identification. This method has been successfully commercialized in self-driving applications by one of the paper authors' company, Nuance Vison. This work has been recognized by an Outstanding Paper Award at ICLR 2021 and has inspired various extensions and related contributions. We have over 20 citation sources in Google Scholar. In response to this difficulty, we propose a novel framework that leverages quantum machine learning for simplification. Our method employs two main components: a quantum processor for precise configuration of each fragment and a classical neural network that learns the individual fragments' behavior. Once the quantum processor has determined the optimal parameters for each fragment, the classical neural network can use this information to predict the compound's ground state with minimal error, even in cases where the fragments' electronic configurations are complex and there are substantial interactions between them. In our example scenarios, we show that this approach delivers high accuracy for molecules like carbon dioxide, water, and boron nitride, and that our model's performance improves with additional data. Furthermore, this framework allows us to investigate how chemical properties change across different fragments and their combinations, thereby enabling the discovery of unexpected properties in compounds. This advancement paves the way for more comprehensive simulations of complex compounds and potentially even large biochemical systems. In addition to this work, we have introduced a public database that provides open-access to quantum simulations, machine learning models, and chemical datasets, and has incorporated contributions from multiple research groups. Together, we have demonstrated the effectiveness of our approach against a more conventional quantum simulation method and have made the source code available on a publicly accessible GitHub repository. In conjunction with the provided dataset, we have facilitated a competition among different quantum algorithm variants, machine learning models, and classical simulation methods. These conditions rely on the presence of specific substructures within the graph. Additionally, we present an algorithm that determines whether a given cubic graph features ideal 3-colourings (both those inducing perfect matchings and those requiring the fewest colours), and we establish a connection between these ideal 3-colourings and certain Hamiltonian cycles and matchings. The provided proof is a corollary to a more general theorem regarding the block structures within certain types of solvable lattices. This paper introduces a new method called Timeloops for automating system call filtering policies in containerized applications. During operation, Timeloops can automatically determine the system calls a program should be permitted to make and prevent unauthorized system calls from being made. In addition, Timeloops rectifies various shortcomings of static analysis-based techniques, such as the creation of highly precise filters for programs in languages like JavaScript, PHP, and Python. Developed using standard, reliable technologies, Timeloops features a simple and effective design that facilitates the integration of additional security modules, making it an adaptable security solution. Our experimental results demonstrate that Timeloops delivers superior performance when compared to alternative solutions. Furthermore, Timeloops has been integrated into the Chronos cluster scheduling framework to provide system call filtering for scalable microservices applications. Our study shows that Timeloops' security efficacy is comparable to that of static analysis-based techniques, while also significantly improving program performance and reducing the system call overhead in multi-node configurations. Our code has been made open source and is available on GitHub under the Apache License, Version 2.0. With the development of cloud computing technologies rapidly advancing, our innovative system call filtering method, Timeloops, has significant implications for improving the security of cloud applications. In particular, Timeloops addresses various security vulnerabilities related to system call manipulation and malicious program behavior, thus making it a ground-breaking solution for cloud service providers and further research into the subject area. In 2021, we released an updated version of Timeloops, now referred to as Chronos-SF, that combines Chronos cluster scheduling software with system call filtering functionality based on static analysis. However, we observed that this approach has several limitations, notably its inability to effectively manage program errors resulting from insufficient system resources, as well as its failure to prevent certain security breaches and program crashes. Consequently, we overhauled the system call filtering module in Chronos-SF from static analysis-based to Timeloops, the new reference implementation. With this change, program error recovery and security enhancement features, including certain attacks prevention and program crash avoidance, were fully integrated into the updated version of Timeloops. Furthermore, our experimental results show that the reimplementation of Timeloops delivers superior performance when compared to Chronos-SF using the previous method. Last but not least, our study demonstrates that the integrated security solutions for system call filtering and program error recovery provide exceptional performance, security, and reliability in multi-node configurations. The success of a soccer match largely depends on the players' actions in critical situations.  Despite significant progress in video games and artificial intelligence, developing a robotic soccer player with high performance in critical situations remains a challenge.  We believe that achieving this goal requires a robot that can adapt to different environment conditions and make informed decisions quickly.  To tackle this issue, we used a deep reinforcement learning method to train a robotic soccer player to perform well in two critical situations: penalty kicks and free kicks.  To ensure the reliability of our results, we conducted multiple trials with varying environment conditions and found that our approach led to a significant improvement in the player's scoring rate and reduction in missed opportunities.  Our experiments also demonstrated that a system combining deep reinforcement learning and robust control can result in a more efficient and effective learning process.  We hope that our findings will contribute to the development of optimal strategies for robotic soccer in the future.  We have attached our source code to this report for reference. By approximating the Earth as smoothly changing, we can use asymptotic ray-theory based solutions to simplify these problems. Since seismic data is typically sampled at short intervals, small-scale variations can cause significant difficulties. To improve the accuracy of extended source imaging, we propose modifying the data and estimated wave field to account for these small-scale variations. We then apply an alternative formula for calculating the imaging operator, one that takes advantage of the extended source data but does so under more favorable conditions. Initial results show that this approach yields acceptable images when compared to the more complicated methods. Further testing is needed to validate these findings. We've demonstrated another method for creating optical asymmetry, achieving this effect not by applying a biased light source or specific photon state but rather through the application of quantum squeezing in one of the signal and idler beams from an OPA.  We showed that applying quantum squeezing to one of these beams results in a significant shift in the system's symmetry, demonstrated through an extreme growth in optical asymmetry when quantum squeezing is applied to the lower-intensity idler beam rather than the more intensely emitted signal beam.  We attribute this phenomenon to the influence of quantum squeezing on the system's two-mode squeezing state.  We also established a method for controlling the degree of optical asmetry through parameters of the OPA, such as optical loss in the system.  Furthermore, we found that even minimal levels of quantum loss can significantly impede the system's ability to achieve high levels of optical asmetry.  Finally, we propose a novel method for detecting optical asmetry based on homodyne detection of one of the beams from the OPA.  We conclude by discussing the implications of our findings for the broader application of quantum phenomena in optical systems.  Specifically, we note that quantum squeezing has the potential to enhance a range of effects in optical systems beyond optical asmetry, making its integration a promising area of research.  We also suggest that the state of an OPA's output beams may be considered a form of entangled photon pair state with optical asmetry, a concept with useful applications in fields like quantum chemistry and physics.  However, further research is needed to fully explore and understand the complexities of this state.  In terms of experimental implementation, our findings suggest that even the relatively simple OPA system we modeled has the capacity for a wide range of phenomena resulting from the interaction of quantum states, making it an ideal subject for study.  However, achieving the high levels of quantum squeezing required to produce significant optical asmetry may be a more complicated process than we've outlined in this theoretical analysis.  Further research is needed to fully understand the potential of quantum-squeezed states in optical systems. Timing and spectral data from the decline phase of the outburst revealed the spin period to be 12.485 seconds, with significant spectral features. A Quasi Periodic Oscillation was observed at a frequency of 0.032 Hz and an RMS amplitude of 18%. Additionally, a low-frequency Spectral State Transition was noted, possibly linked to the partial accretion of the outer disk due to the binary's large mass ratio. Recently proposed programmable phase plates offer promising potential in advancing transmission electron microscopy (TEM). By allowing the precise control of electron phase accumulation, they have the capacity to significantly enhance image contrast and resolution. Nevertheless, their implementation faces a critical challenge: the difficulty of accurately correcting for electron wavefront distortion during their passage through the microscope column. This issue becomes particularly pronounced at higher acceleration voltages. The impact of electron phase accumulation along the microscope column needs to be thoroughly considered and its effects mitigated through appropriate phase plate design or the incorporation of a corrective phase function. By examining the electron phase accumulation in the TEM column, our research reveals the inability of conventional phase plates to fully address this issue. In response, we propose an alternative design featuring a double-layer electron phase plate. Through numerical simulations, we demonstrate its capability to counteract the electron wavefront distortion experienced during its passage through the microscope column, thus potentially enabling the effective use of high-voltage electrons in TEM without the need for electron beam phase modulation. Our results also indicate that a programmable phase plate with a corrective phase function can provide improved image quality and high-resolution detail, comparable to that achieved with an unprogrammed phase plate at lower acceleration voltages. However, its design parameters must be carefully matched to the characteristics of the electron beam and the microscope column. Our research provides valuable insights for the optimal design of programmable phase plates, enabling them to function as effective aberration correctors in the TEM. Our findings are relevant to all TEMs that employ electron phase plates, regardless of their acceleration voltage capabilities. Our numerical simulations demonstrate the potential of double-layer electron phase plates to enhance image quality and resolution in TEM. Our research may also contribute valuable knowledge to the development of optimized electron optics in other electron microscopy techniques, such as electron energy-loss spectroscopy. While it is common to evaluate the generated text for its semantic and syntactic quality, the underlying representation of this encoding is often overlooked, which can hinder the model's performance in anticipating the next utterance. This work argues that merely assessing text generation metrics from human or automated sources is insufficient in gauging a model's understanding of dialogue language, prompting the proposal of a set of evaluation tasks to scrutinize the encoder representations used in these models. Speech generation with limited context poses a significant challenge, as existing models rely on extensive context to produce realistic and accurate outputs. This problem is particularly pronounced in applications requiring context-aware speech generation, such as virtual assistants and chatbots. To address this, we introduce MaskedSpeech, a novel speech generation model that utilizes a unique masking strategy to incorporate context through a series of connected chunks. This strategy enables the model to efficiently process limited context by exploiting linguistic properties, such as syntactic coherence and lexical connectivity. Our experimental evaluations reveal that MaskedSpeech achieves exceptional performance compared to baseline models, surpassing them in terms of disfluency reduction, semantic coherence, and user acceptability. Notably, MaskedSpeech demonstrates comparable performance to state-of-the-art models like Transformervs and Generation models when provided with ample context, yet it excels in context-aware speech generation using limited context. Our code and models are publicly available for download. This work introduces a pioneering context-aware speech generation framework that outperforms existing models, especially when applied to real-world applications involving limited context. This includes (1) speech data prepping, (2) text-to-speech tasks, and (3) virtual human interactions. In various image processing tasks, including video compressed sensing and color image demosaicing, images must be decompressed or deblurred to continue processing. A crucial step in both processes involves solving a multichannel image reconstruction problem from a single channel. By leveraging the properties of circular convolution and the demosaicing process, we transform this problem into a separable one, utilizing a specific convolutional matrix product property. Specifically, we express the compressed or blurred image as the product of several factors, including the compressed sensing matrix, convolution filters, and the original image, arranged in a specific order. This comprehension enables us to devise new methods for estimating the missing color channels, including a straightforward approach based on code augmentation, a more advanced method that employs code augmentation in an iterative process, and a codeaugmentated alternating direction method that leverages our previous research on ADMM. We provide a comprehensive evaluation of these new methods, including codeaugmentated iterations, in a simulated compressed video scenario. Our results demonstrate that codeaugmentated iterations yield superior performance, outperforming even state-of-the-art algorithms like ANR. By transforming the compressive video reconstruction problem into a separable one, we exploit the benefits of codeaugmentated iterations to achieve a more significant improvement in PSNR than previous methods. Ultimately, our codeaugmentated approaches exhibit better performance than traditional and contemporary algorithms in both demosaicing and compressed video reconstruction tasks. Our code has been made publicly available for download. Moreover, we provide a numerical solution to the convolved compressed sensing problem, allowing us to apply codeaugmentated iterations directly. This solution facilitates the use of any optimization method that can handle a specific form of variation. Our work offers a new perspective on compressed sensing and signal processing, and we are confident that our code and approaches will be valuable resources for future research. By combining transit observations from NASA's TESS and high-resolution, radial velocity measurements from the Keck, we aim to explore the relationship between exoplanet density and several key variables in a comprehensive study.  To execute this investigation, we will focus on specific target groups, including those with host stars similar to the Sun, small low-mass stars, and large evolved stars.  For each target subset, we will examine how density relates to several factors such as the temperature of the host star, the orbital period of the planet, and the distance from the host star to the planet.  To carry out this study, we will use a statistical analysis method to eliminate any biases that might stem from observing conditions and select 50 potential targets from the vast pool of suitable transit events detected by TESS.  Ultimately, our research will provide a framework for integrating transit light curve and radial velocity data, shedding light on the many variables that influence a planet's density. By analyzing Herschel Space Observatory data from a survey of the solar system, we obtained the flux values for three asteroids: (10115) 1992 SK, (1685) Toro, and (1620) Geographos. Determining the physical characteristics of M-dwarfs is crucial for studying low-mass stars and planet host stars. This paper presents a new sample of 245 non-binary M-dwarfs, and outlines a data-driven approach to assess their stellar parameters. By comparing their properties to those of 6250 nearby M-dwarfs with established parameters, we establish a set of default parameters that can be applied to the sample stars until more precise measurements are obtained for each individual star. This technique's effectiveness is demonstrated through a subset of 54 exoplanet host stars, and their calculated parameters are consistent with those reported in previous studies. However, our analysis reveals some discrepancies in the parameters reported by the California-Kepler Survey, and our method provides a more precise and uniform dataset that can be used for future studies of these star systems. Additionally, we identify 8 stars with potential temperature anomalies, and 5 stars with potential mass anomalies. Our approach to evaluating the sample's stellar parameters will lay the groundwork for analyzing the planets orbiting these stars. Furthermore, our results highlight the need for more precise stellar parameters when detecting and analyzing exoplanet transit light curves and radial velocity data. In a subsequent paper, we will utilize this sample to investigate the relationship between star mass and the probability of hosting a small planet. Additionally, we will examine how the likelihood of a star being visible from Earth affects the distribution of small planets as a function of mass. Our data shows that there is a 5.6 times greater likelihood of finding a small planet around a star that can be seen from Earth, and this enhancement in planet prevalence decreases with increasing stellar mass. Moreover, we found that the distribution of small planets in our sample is consistent with that of larger planets, and there is a threshold to the density of such planets in a given mass range. Lastly, our research demonstrates that there is a bias in existing planet detection programs that favor the detection of low-mass planets around stars that are easily visible from Earth. Nonetheless, the field of M-dwarfs is vast, and a significant portion of its stars remain untargeted by current planet hunting methods. Therefore, we suggest that future exoplanet hunting programs, such as that of the TEPCO mission, consider incorporating a more comprehensive approach when selecting targets. This strategy should prioritize a wide range of M-dwarfs over binary systems and stars with established planets, and take advantage of breakthroughs in astronomical techniques that allow for the detection of exoplanets beyond the Earth's distance from these star systems

The underlying principles of the ventral temporal cortex's organization in the back of the brain were long thought to be shaped by living entities' visual characteristics. A prominent theory proposes that this organization is rooted in a fundamental distinction made by this sensory system: the difference between animate and inanimate objects. Recent studies have made notable contributions to our understanding of this phenomenon; however, the existing literature is fragmented and requires integration to fully grasp the current state of knowledge and the underlying mechanisms of this phenomenon. Advanced computational models based on deep neural networks offer valuable insights into the complex patterns in visual data and the cortex's organizational structure. We utilized a state-of-the-art deep network designed to recognize characters, animals, and vehicles from images and analyzed its layers to gain a deeper understanding of the animate-inanimate dimension in the human visual cortex. Our findings reveal that a robust, high-level representation of visual data is composed of multiple distinct features that are capable of grasping the general category of living entities from lower-level details that can recognize specific characteristics of animals. Moreover, this composite representation is more resistant to variations in visual data than its individual components. Our study provides a comprehensive explanation for previous findings and offers a practical example of how a deep network's layers can be used to explore complex phenomena in the human visual cortex. A uniform analysis approach was applied to photometric data within the F257 to F1645 wavelength range. The mass-to-light ratios of the clusters were calculated through luminosity-based mass estimates, and a simple model was used to determine radii by assuming a distance of 10 kpc for all galaxies. The calculated radii range from approximately 2 to 14 parsecs, showing little correlation with cluster mass or mass-to-light ratio. This led to a significant revision of the radii of the most massive clusters in the sample, reducing their mean radius by approximately 50 percent. This revised understanding of cluster geometry has implications for the use of mass-to-light ratios as a tool for studying the dark matter content of nearby galaxies. A prominent paradigm in reward learning utilizes inverse reinforcement learning to derive optimal rewards from human demonstrations.  Despite the effectiveness of this approach, its broad adoption is hindered by the time-consuming and subjective nature of human ranking across diverse state spaces.  To address this issue, we introduce a new method called Visually Aided Cluster Ranking (VisACR), which leverages vision-based techniques to efficiently utilize human feedback.  VisACR divides the state space into clusters and seeks human input to rank only the representative states within each cluster.  To assign states to clusters based on these rankings, VisACR employs a data-driven method called Visually Aided Clustering (VisAC), which minimizes the variance of ranks within each cluster.  We demonstrate that human-provided data for VisACR is substantially shorter than what is required for traditional methods.  Furthermore, our results indicate that VisACR achieves comparable and sometimes superior performance to baseline methods using reinforcement learning and inverse reinforcement learning.  We also show that VisACR's clusters correspond to distinct regions of the state space as defined by a state representation that is optimal for reinforcement learning.  We publicly release our code and data at https://github.com/gualtiero-viscriani/visacr. Structural preferences in a language's word order can vary greatly depending on the type of verb and the level of conformance (concord) it exhibits with other verbs in the same sentence.  Conformance in some languages, such as Basque, is quite strict with respect to verb placement and conformance (cascading conformance).  Studying how well sequence models, like Last Maximum Attention networks, learn to replicate these patterns from data through cascading conformance has yielded interesting insights.  Our analysis indicates that these models can pick up on certain patterns but also exhibit a significant degree of unpredictability in their behavior, often producing counterintuitive outcomes and significant deviations from the expected distribution of sentence structures.  Additionally, we find that the degree of unpredictability varies depending on the type of verb and the level of conformance, with a interesting interaction between the two.  To better comprehend how sequence models grasp relational patterns in semantics and syntax, our results highlight the importance of further examination of the ways in which they handle cascading conformance.  To facilitate this examination, we introduce Verbspace, a visual representation of pre-trained verb knowledge that can be learned from data, providing an easily accessible overview of a language's verb structure and the variability of its dependencies.  With Verbspace, we show that the knowledge it represents is closely linked to the vocabulary's intrinsic properties and that it can be used to identify unique aspects of a language's syntax.  Furthermore, we demonstrate the versatility of Verbspace by using it to investigate a wide range of structural preferences in Basque and show that it can be expanded to include other sequence models, like BERT and T5.  Ultimately, Verbspace is a valuable resource for any exploration or analysis of the verb knowledge that sequence models gain from data.  To facilitate this examination, Verbspace is a publicly available tool that can be accessed at the provided website.  In addition to Verbspace, we have made all the verb datasets used in our experiments, along with all the experiments conducted with them, available for any researcher or practitioner to use in their own work.  On a broader level, our work contributes to the ongoing discussion about the potential differences between neural network-based models and the underlying assumptions of the systematicity hypothesis, laying out a concrete framework for testing some of these assumptions.  Furthermore, our research offers a unique method for evaluating the reliability of state-of-the-art neural network-based language models, along with a new metric for measuring the variability of a language's syntax.

A novel spin-singlet topological superfluid (STSF) is proposed in a model that incorporates Rashba spin-orbit coupling and a two-dimensional Rashba Hubbard model with attractive interaction.  Employing a strong-coupling approach and Monte Carlo simulations, we demonstrate that this model exhibits spin-singlet topological superfluidity at the mean-field level and also confirms this result through the inclusion of electron correlations.  Furthermore, we identify the underlying physics governing STSF in this model, specifically the role of Rashba spin-orbit coupling in creating a topological insulator, and analyze the associated transport properties using a five-dimensional effective action.  Our findings suggest that the STSF state can be characterized by transport measurements of the spin-polarized conductance and the correlation between electron's spin and its orbital momentum.  We anticipate that this model, which is relevant to research on Rashba superfluids, can be realized with ultracold atoms trapped in optical lattices under the influence of spin-orbit coupling and magnetic fields.  We also outline the parameters required for this system to exhibit STSF and the necessary techniques for detecting this state through transport measurements.  Therefore, this model provides an ideal platform for exploring the physics of Rashba superfluids and the effects of spin-orbit coupling in atomic gases. Theories explaining highly elongated polymer brush properties have provided valuable insights yet are limited in application due to their restrictive geometric assumptions. A new mathematical approach is developed to analyze the morphology of molten polymer brushes regardless of their shape, generating a comprehensive theory that explains the emergence of exclusion zones in strongly stretched brushes. A key feature of this theory is its ability to be applied to brushes in arbitrary strong stretching states, challenging a previous model's limitation to only understanding the dynamics of brush brushes on the cusp of a phase change. A key innovation of this approach involves representing brush interactions through field theories that capture the intricate details of polymer-surface and polymer-polymer interactions. By incorporating a detailed analysis of the geometry of arbitrary brushes, a new scaling for their dimensions is derived, offering a precise mathematical description of the phase diagram and brush morphology. A key prediction of this model is the existence of exclusion zones in brushes under strong stretch conditions, along with a critical regime where brushes exhibit coexistence of flat and highly elongated configurations. The developed approach also sheds light on the role of surface curvature in brushes under marginal adhesion conditions, revealing a universal scaling for brush dimensions and a geometric explanation for the previously observed feature of enhanced tackiness in small particles. We introduce a new variant of the minimum dimension concept known as the trimmed metric dimension for graphs. Unlike traditional dimension theories, our dim_p_ framework excludes specific graph vertices from being part of the reference set, R. Subsequently, we establish the trimmed dimension of a graph, dim_p_(G)_t, by identifying the minimum number of vertices, p, required to pinpoint all other vertices in a graph G, using a reference set that excludes at most t vertices from G. Our explorations include a preliminary analysis of the trimmed metric dimension of various graph classes, particularly focus on certain types of graphs with particular properties, as well as an investigation into the relationship between dim_p_(G)_t and the trimmed version of another concept known as the bipartite dimension. Finally, we provide a method for determining the trimmed dimension of a graph by formulating it as an NP-complete problem and subsequently establishing a connection to a similar variant of another famous problem. Additionally, we present lower and upper bounds for the trimmed dimension of some graph classes, including what the dimension would be if no vertices were excluded, which is essentially the standard dimension concept. Last but not least, we ask some open questions to encourage further exploration into this newly introduced concept. Researchers explored a novel use for machine learning image processing algorithms, applying them to all-sky maps generated by the Fermi Gamma-ray Space Telescope. To create these images, data from the Large Area Telescope are grouped into energy bins and processed through a technique called count-to-flux conversion, which incorporates the effective collecting area and energy response of the telescope. This conversion step introduces noise and a non-linear transformation of the data, making image processing challenging. To overcome this difficulty, researchers developed a novel approach involving a residual neural network, combining a generator network with a latent variable. This model first estimates the median all-sky map in a specific energy range, followed by the estimation of unusual sources. When trained on 12 energy bins using a large dataset of 3.5 years of observation, the model demonstrated an ability to recover detailed features of these unusual sources. One example of such a source is the Cygnus X-1, a bright binary system known for its gamma-ray emissions. By highlighting gamma-ray emissions from this source, the model can effectively identify it in the all-sky maps. Another example is the gamma-ray binary system G309.87+00.58, which the model discovered in the Milky Way's center through its detection of unusual sources. This discovery technique offers a promising alternative method for identifying variable sources, such as gamma-ray binaries, and the model's performance can be further improved using more advanced machine learning algorithms. This novel approach to image processing can also be applied to other telescopes and observational data. A subset of tasks that forms a path in the graph is known as a serial task sequence. We are given a set of workers, each with a distinct capability set, and the ability to assign tasks to workers in a serial manner. The goal is to determine the maximum subset of compatible tasks that can be completed by assigning them to the workers in a serial order. This problem remains NP-hard, even with limited constraints such as a single worker available. We developed an open-source software called Binary Aster Detection System, which utilizes pre-existing image processing techniques and mathematical methods to identify binary asteroids within wide-field optical images. Specifically, we based our approach on existing algorithms and incorporated their features to pinpoint potential binary asteroid candidates and assess their likelihood of involvement in the YORP effect, which generates a varying spin speed in asteroids rotating binary bodies. To test our detection method, we applied it to a dataset of 204 near-Earth asteroids, of which our software identified 12 previously known binary or related asteroids and 14 candidates awaiting confirmation through direct observations or other data sources. To evaluate our algorithm's effectiveness, we conducted a simulation showing it can correctly identify 75% of binary asteroids and 90% of their variants when using real data from the Pan-STARRS1 survey. We encourage other researchers to review and use our publicly available detection code, which we based on established methods to efficiently identify binary asteroids from wide-field optical images. We plan to expand our approach to analyze images from the upcoming Luci Sky Survey, which will specialize in detecting binary and other unusual asteroids. Due to its wide field of view and high sensitivity, Luci is expected to discover numerous binary asteroids, leading the way in a new generation of astronomical surveys. To better understand the binary asteroid population, we will refine our detection method to retrieve related information from archival images, particularly those showing unusual light curves associated with rotating binary asteroids. Such data will be valuable for studying these bodies' physical characteristics, including their shape, spin speed, and orbital interactions. To that end, we will use our detection code on a dataset of 3,200 asteroids with available light curves from the Pan-STARRS1 Archival Images, which we will filter based on their orbital paths, spin speeds, and shape-related features. We will also explore linking our detection method with existing modeling software to analyze the retrieved data sets and reconstruct the binary asteroids' physical properties. Furthermore, we will incorporate our detection algorithm into the upcoming Luci Sky Survey's data analysis process to identify binary asteroids and related bodies, which will contribute to a more comprehensive understanding of the binary asteroid population and its variation according to orbital paths. Additionally, we will use our detection code as a baseline for comparing the detection performance of different algorithms, which will be beneficial for identifying areas for improving the detection of binary asteroids. The Southern Atlantic rift system developed as a mid-ocean ridge during late Cretaceous to early Paleogene times, extending approximately 6400 km from the South American to the African continent.  This study offers a comprehensive analysis of oceanic and continental rift margins using a multi-dimensional approach that combines observations from seismic data, ship-based magnetic measurements, and bathymetric mapping.  Initial rifting in the South Atlantic began around 130 million years ago in the southern region, with rifting progressing northward over time.  However, significant oceanic accretion at mid-ocean ridges didn't occur until around 120 million years ago in the southern section and 110 million years ago in the northern section.  This delay in seafloor creation in the northern section is believed to have resulted in reduced rifting activity and the failure of rifting in West Africa and Brazil during late Cretaceous to early Paleogene times.  This failure to rift is linked to increased rifting in East Africa and the Red Sea, with rifting in these areas occurring at a later time than in West Africa.  As a result, East Africa experienced right-lateral motion and the extensional features in West Africa were offset, with this offset featured as a 2000 km-wide zone of shear in the Earth's mantle.  This shear zone in the mantle caused the failed rifting in West Africa and Brazil to shift to a more easterly longitude in the continent, with this failure to rift also influencing sedimentary basin development in South America.  This failure to rift in West Africa and Brazil had long-lasting effects, with this episode of mantle shearing producing a range of features, including the Rio Grande Rise, the Discovery Seamounts, and the Falkland Islands.  It also influenced oceanic and continental crust creation in the Southern Atlantic by altering the composition of this crust from extended to normal or even oceanic-continental crust in the southern section, with this change then moving northward over time. It also led to a greater variety of oceanic and continental crust creation in the Southern Atlantic than would have occurred if rifting had proceeded at a uniform rate across this region. Word meanings can be altered by changes in culture, geography, and personal beliefs, resulting in distinct understandings of the same words.  Due to the limited nature of existing resources, automatically identifying words with varying meanings is a complex task.  Our research uncovers a new approach, called VD, for discovering words with different semantic meanings.  Based on the underlying theory that similar meaning variations can be captured in the same semantic vector space, we take a data-driven approach.  We extract implicit meaning variations by identifying pairs of equivalent statements with different word order.  Then, we apply and experiment with this method on two datasets, finding that a word will be flagged as having varying meaning in approximately 15% of cases.  Our results suggest that this method is a promising means of discovering words with different semantic meanings.  Due to limitations in existing resources, such as word sense inventories, there is a need for more comprehensive approaches to understanding word meanings. We investigated the parameters of Early Dark Energy (EDE) models using a comprehensive dataset that includes cosmic microwave background (CMB) data from Planck and a large set of large-scale structure data from the Baryon Oscillation Spectroscopic Survey (BOSS). Our analysis revealed specific constraints on EDE models, including a critical limit on the EDE density fraction relative to the present-day dark energy density, with a specific condition applied to avoid model inconsistencies. This limit indicates that the EDE density must have been very small, at a level significantly more restrictive than previous estimates, especially in models where the matter density is low. This newly discovered limit holds significant implications for models aiming to explain early universe phenomena, such as the generation of primordial gravitational waves, and suggests these models will face a major challenge in reconciling their predictions with observations of the early universe. Additionally, we found that a previously reported feature in the lithium abundance data, which could be linked to EDE models, is not compatible with the more stringent constraints imposed by the Planck and BOSS data. However, we found that a different EDE model, one with a slightly delayed matter dominance phase, can successfully explain this phenomenon and, as a result, this model's density fraction, while still quite small, is consistent with the constraints imposed by the Planck and BOSS data. Nonetheless, this variant of an EDE model with a delayed matter dominance phase still represents a departure from the standard cosmological model that governed the early universe and its evolution. Moreover, even though this model's density fraction, although still quite small, is consistent with the constraints imposed by the Planck and BOSS data, it still represents a departure from the standard cosmological model that governed the early universe and its evolution. This method, however, yielded slightly different numerical values for the EDE density fraction, although the overall constraint remains the same. Nonetheless, both analytical and numerical methods reach the same conclusion, that the EDE density must have been very small, at a level significantly more restrictive than previous estimates, especially in models where the matter density is low. reasoning skill that can be critical in complex scenarios involving multiple
elements. Although current LLMs excel at individual element reasoning, their
performance drops when these elements are combined in a single sentence.
Importantly, because many real-world applications involve combining elements
within a single sentence, such as in political debate or discussion forums,
there is a significant need to investigate how to use LLMs for this type of
reasoning. In our research, we introduce an innovative approach called
DISCO, a method that uses a variety of LLM-based tools to automatically generate
a simplified, phrasal-level explanation of why a sentence is true or false.
We demonstrate that not only human evaluators find these explanations more
coherent and relevant than chance, but also that they often match the level
of complexity of the original sentence. Moreover, we show that when incorporating
these explanations back into the LLM, they see a notable boost in performance,
even when tested on new, unseen data. In effect, this means that by using a
variety of LLM-based methods, we can significantly improve the ability of LLMs

disentanglement techniques to a single sentence, and discover that this leads

further exploration of a broader range of comprehension and reasoning tasks.

Nevertheless, successful distant growth requires overcoming substantial energy barriers associated with nucleation and island formation. One approach to achieving this is by utilizing Heusler compounds, which can exhibit exceptional magnetic and electrical properties.
