Rounding is an important phenomenon affecting the collection of sensitive information, particularly when it comes to counting sensitive events. While research exists on people's behavior when responding to questions about the number of units on a specific scale, far less is known about responses that involve estimating a total count based on rounded averages of individual items. This study addresses this gap by examining a scenario in which participants estimate a total count by averaging a series of numbers, where each number represents the quantity of a particular item and must be rounded to the nearest integer. The average is then multiplied by the total number of items to obtain an estimate of the total count. What makes this scenario complex is that it involves a non-linear transformation of rounded values, which may lead to inaccurate estimates due to the effects of rounding. The impact of this phenomenon is evaluated over different ranges of possible values and estimates, and strategies are presented for collecting such data when a well-known method is not feasible. The results indicate that the loss of accuracy varies based on the range of data being collected, and several approaches were developed to enhance the precision of estimates in cases where the standard method of collection is not available. Researchers investigated the crystal and magnetic characteristics of single-crystal GdInO3 through a combined approach using synchrotron X-ray diffraction, resistivity, and magnetic susceptibility in a broad range of temperatures and magnetic fields. GdInO3 exhibits a temperature-induced transition from a paramagnetic to a long-range-ordered magnetic state, which occurs at a critical temperature that varies depending on the direction and intensity of the applied magnetic field. When studied under high-field, low-temperature conditions, researchers discovered a distinct resistance minimum and a corresponding magnetic-susceptibility maximum, which indicate the presence of a topological transition in this material. A numerical simulation using a 4x4x1 lattice structure accurately models the observed properties of GdInO3. This model comprises two weakly coupled quasi-two-dimensional honeycomb layers and accurately predicts the observed resistance minimum and magnetic-susceptibility maximum. A comparison of experimental data and theoretical predictions reveals a small discrepancy in the spin-susceptibility maximum, which indicates a slight anisotropy in the spin structure of this material. A new theoretical threshold for the spin-susceptibility maximum is proposed, and it is anticipated that future adjustments to the model will provide a more precise fit between experimental and theoretical data. Researchers propose that further optimization of the model will yield a more accurate comparison with experimental data, and this could lead to a better understanding of the spin structure of GdInO3. Those conclusions are consistent with the results of this study, and they collectively provide a comprehensive understanding of the complex magnetic characteristics of GdInO3. In our research, we diverge from the standard practice in unsupervised domain adaptation (UDA) of relying on a direct, certain link between source and target domains. We instead leverage stochastic connections, capturing the random associations between the domains. This approach is implemented via a novel method using conditional entropy, which penalizes discordant samples in the target domain. We achieve this by introducing a new penalty term in the optimization process. The proposed technique is shown to overcome the limitations of current UDA methods, notably successful class-indiscriminate adaptation, by explicitly discouraging target domain labels that are unlikely given the source domain. The effectiveness of this approach is validated across multiple benchmark datasets for UDA, resulting in notable performance improvements over existing methods. Notably, our approach is particularly effective in scenarios where the source and target domains have minimal overlap, significantly reducing errors by a substantial margin of 12.3% in cases of high discrepancy. The proposed algorithm and experiments are readily replicable thanks to our open-source code availability. The code can be downloaded at https://github.com/ghush20/BSDA. The statistical results of our experiments are also available online at https://www.dropbox.com/s/6m0s1u1f9h5mr0s/extra.pdf?dl=0. The proposed approach has the potential to address random source-target domain connections, a prevalent issue in real-world scenarios, by providing a more versatile framework for UDA. A narrow, spiral galaxy called UGC 8839, located approximately 540 million light-years from Earth, has been the subject of prior studies. However, researchers have discovered that Hubble Space Telescope observations reveal a previously unseen, highly stable ring in this galaxy. The ring, dubbed the "hyper-stable disk", exhibits exceptional rigidity and lacks the typical star formation found in other ring features of galaxies. The unique characteristics of this ring may be attributed to a minor merger that occurred around 50 million years ago, or possibly more recently, which could have contributed to the ring's formation and maintenance. The ring's inactivity suggests that it is isolated from the galaxy's central dynamic zone and may be a dormant feature waiting to interact with the surrounding environment. Furthermore, the discovery of compact, ultraluminous X-ray sources and a faint black hole candidate in this galaxy, along with its nearby field of binaries displaying a high X-ray binary ratio, indicate that UGC 8839 possesses a substantial population of binary systems. The galaxy's merger history and large bulge fraction may have contributed to the creation and preservation of its unique ring feature. The discovery of this highly stable ring in UGC 8839 provides valuable insights into the complex processes occurring within galaxies and the effects of cosmic events on binary systems. Ultimately, this finding highlights the importance of observational limits and the potential hidden phenomena waiting to be uncovered through further astronomical research. Theoretical models of galaxy mergers can generate rings similar to UGC 8839's hyper-stable disk, or outer ring structures, at various stages following the merger event. However, these models require a massive disk and a minor merger to produce an inner, highly stable ring like the one found in UGC 8839. This understanding can be utilized to analyze other galaxies displaying ring features, aiding in their analysis and providing a new perspective on the processes occurring within galaxies throughout the universe. The unique features of this galaxy, including its hyper-stable disk, suggest that celestial mergers have the ability to activate or reactivate dormant binary systems located at the outer edges of galaxies. This process may result in the creation of unusual, highly energetic objects such as ULX sources, which can provide valuable insights into the complex interactions between galaxies and their surrounding environments. Ancient detectors, or "paleo-detectors," hold historical value and technological significance from the early days of radiation detection. These devices, often used for medical isotope detection, were exposed to environmental radiation until the present day and provide a unique historical radiation exposure record. Due to their age and environmental exposure, the amounts of certain types of radiation detected by these devices are hundreds to thousands of times lower than modern detection limits, allowing for the investigation of extremely low levels of radiation. As a result, ancient detectors offer an innovative approach to searching for dark matter interactions at a very low scale, potentially below existing limits set by other experiments. Using a comprehensive list of paleo-detectors containing sources of environmental radiation exposure and their exposure times, we perform a detailed analysis to determine the current limits set by these detectors for the two dark matter processes, neutrino loss and electromagnetic interaction. Our study finds that future improvements in detection technology could significantly enhance the sensitivity of these devices, often by one to two orders of magnitude, which could reach the COMET/DMTPC experiment's current limits by the year 2030 and surpass them by 2035. Although the statistical significance of a signal in ancient detectors would depend on various factors, their historical value makes a positive finding compelling, with a finding of $3\sigma$ or greater significance by 2030 corresponding to a much lower exposure limit, which would imply a significantly more profound discovery. Additionally, we highlight that the limits set by these devices can be achieved with minimal financial investment and without the need for large-scale research facilities, making them an affordable and accessible alternative to existing dark matter detection methods. However, the achievable exposure limits to which we can sensitively detect with these devices rely on several assumptions and rely on further research into the historical operation and technical specifications of these devices. Nonetheless, we believe that using ancient detectors as a means of searching for dark matter interactions represents a pioneering approach with significant scientific value and technological significance. As such, we hope that our study will serve as an incentive for researchers to explore this uncharted area of study and uncover the historical secrets hidden within ancient detectors. Additionally, we hope that our analysis will provide a useful framework for the scientific community to build upon in further investigating the capabilities of these historical devices. With regard to the theoretical aspects of this study, we hope that our analysis will contribute to a better comprehension of the existing and future limits set by these detectors in detecting dark matter and will provide a foundation for the examination of other novel methods of detecting dark matter. This paper introduces a novel solution, DP-Sync, that addresses the challenge of maintaining confidentiality for user update patterns in cloud-based databases. Our proposed approach achieves this confidentiality through the application of differential privacy, enabling users to securely update databases in the cloud by concealing their update history. To facilitate fast query processing, DP-Sync updates the database in two phases, initially performing an unrestricted update and later applying a private transformation to ensure differential privacy is maintained. A further innovation of this work includes the incorporation of multiple descriptions of user updates, allowing for the efficient private publication of statistical aggregates of updates. Comprehensive experiments conducted on real-world datasets demonstrate DP-Sync's effectiveness in ensuring differential privacy and its practical capabilities for supporting efficient and secure update operations and query processing in cloud databases. The extensive use of Machine Learning (ML) in high-security sectors necessitates a transparent understanding of its methodology. Nonetheless, research into decoding ML models like Random Forest is in its nascent stages. To bridge this knowledge gap, we employ rigorous mathematical techniques and logical reasoning to create a pioneering method for explaining the predictions made by Random Forest. Our approach revolves around Minimal Unsatisfiable Cores and incorporates two key features to enhance prediction insight: 1) identifying the most crucial attributes used for the prediction and 2) detecting the minimal data points used to train the model. Furthermore, our method recognizes the limitations of these features in isolation and instead, we propose a combined framework that examines the relationship between feature significance and the robustness of models in withstanding adversarial attacks. Re-identifying individuals across different cameras and time points without labels poses a significant challenge in large-scale surveillance scenarios. This task is complicated by factors such as varying pose, face obstruction, and age, which necessitate a robust and flexible surveillance re-identification system. We introduce a novel unsupervised re-identification approach based on contrastive learning, which ensures that identical individuals have similar representations across various images, even if the images differ in appearance. Our method combines contrastive learning with a data augmentation technique called Mixup, which enables a more comprehensive exploration of the individual variability. We test our approach on three large public datasets and find that it achieves superior or comparable performance compared to state-of-the-art unsupervised methods while operating at a significantly better training time. Notably, our approach demonstrates exceptional efficacy in handling age differences, with results showing that it outperforms all current state-of-the-art methods on datasets with age spans of over a decade. Our code is available online at https://github.com/kezhi6/unsupervised_re_id. Additionally, we introduce a new large-scale dataset called Airport365, which comprises over 1 million images and offers a practical application scenario for unsupervised re-identification in real-world surveillance environments. This dataset is unique in its large scale and is now available for public use at https://github.com/kezhi6/Airport365. We also formulate a corresponding evaluation protocol and benchmark for the dataset, which serves as a rigorous standard for benchmarking and assessing the performance of unsupervised re-identification methods. This includes a straightforward protocol for adding new datasets, which can be found in the detailed instructions provided in the appendix. Our results on Airport365 have been added to the final section of this document. They demonstrate that our proposed approach achieves top performance on this dataset. Moreover, we conduct a thorough analysis of the dataset's characteristics and the challenges it presents, along with some practical applications involving personal age re-identification. Lastly, we explore various ways to enhance the performance of the model on this dataset, which includes multiple strategies for incorporating additional information that can aid in the re-identification of individuals. These methods are equally applicable to other large-scale surveillance datasets. We anticipate that our contributions, specifically the introduction of the Mixup+NS method and the evaluation protocol we developed, will greatly contribute to the advancement of surveillance re-identification research. We examine the formation of Population III binary remnants within nuclear star clusters using a semi-analytical model for the early universe. Our framework accounts for the movement of Population III binary remnants during the formation of the universe's structure and identifies which of these remnants fall into nuclear star clusters through gravitational interaction with field Population II stars. Following this, we track the remnants' evolution within these star clusters through gravitational encounters and gravitational waves, and predict the likelihood of their merger into intermediate-mass black holes. Our model shows that nuclear star clusters host $10^{-3}$ to $10^{-5}$ intermediate-mass black holes with a population weight of 0.01 to 1. Conversely, massive halos of the universe contain $10^{-6}$ to $10^{-8}$ intermediate-mass black holes with a population weight of 0.001 to 0.01. Furthermore, we find that nuclear star clusters produce binary Population III mergers at a rate of 0.4 to 5.2 Gpc$^{-3}$ yr$^{-1}$, while massive halos result in binary Population III mergers at a rate of 0.03 to 0.4 Gpc$^{-3}$ yr$^{-1}$. These predictions align with existing observations of optical counterparts of gravitational waves and offer forecasts for future detection of such events. Our model also estimates that the detection of next-generation gravitational wave detectors, such as the Einstein Telescope, will allow for direct detection of Population III binary mergers at a confidence level of 50%. Additionally, we find that the most sensitive parameter of such detectors is the detector's sensitivity to low-frequency signals. Lastly, we provide an updated version of our model that considers the formation of nuclear star clusters as compact quasars, forming Population III binary remnants at a rate of 10 to 100 in every nuclear star cluster. The Gamma-Ray Burst (GRB) simulator employed by the Gravitational wave high-energy Electromagnetic Counterpart All-sky Monitor (GECAM) spacecraft is a compact, portable device that we present in this report. Developed from a conventional Field Programmable Gate Array (FPGA), it mimics the signal characteristics of GRBs and Gamma-Ray Surges (GRS) that the GECAM spacecraft will encounter. The device features a wide frequency band, spanning 5 kHz to 100 kHz, and a variable burst duration ranging from 0.1 seconds to 100 seconds. The firmware is adaptable to accommodate different spacecraft communication protocols and ensures seamless simulation of GRBs and GRS signals. A demonstration of the simulator was held at the 36th Meeting of the Academic Satellite Experiments for Gravitational Wave, during which attendees observed a simulated GRS phenomenon. The device has since been delivered to the Beijing Aerospace Technique Research Center for use in testing the GECAM spacecraft. The portable Gamma-Ray Surge simulator developed by our team has proven a valuable resource for the thorough testing of spacecraft communication systems. The technical details of this project have been shared with the open community to facilitate collaboration and knowledge exchange. The fully functional prototype of the Gamma-Ray Surge simulator is now available for any space mission or scientific research initiative that requires simulation of these phenomena. The corresponding software code has been made publicly accessible on the GitHub platform. The collaborative work on this project has provided an opportunity for students to engage in hands-on learning and participate in the development of a cutting-edge technical solution. The successful integration of this simulator into the development process of the GECAM spacecraft serves as an exemplary model for the effective collaboration between Chinese and international academic institutions and industrial partners. The significant advancements achieved in this project have contributed meaningfully to the completion of the GECAM spacecraft and have paved the way for further cooperation and partnership in the advancement of space science and technology. The pioneering work done on this project has enabled the demonstration of a critical communication function for the GECAM spacecraft in orbit. The innovative approach to problem-solving developed by our team has created a path for the demonstration of a crucial communication function for the GECAM spacecraft in its operational phase. The groundbreaking solution achieved in this project has established a new benchmark for the development of particle detectors and spacecraft communication systems in space science and astronomy. Humanity has long sought a deeper understanding of the world through diverse fields of study, yet a universal framework for measuring progress remains elusive despite numerous attempts. To address this challenge, researchers have tried various methods such as productivity metrics, knowledge graphs, and network analyses to gain insights into the evolution of human knowledge and the effectiveness of scientific endeavors. Here, we introduce a novel approach that combines these methods with a unique framework for evaluation, which we apply to a broad spectrum of disciplines spanning 350 years. Here, we outline our findings on the current state of scientific productivity and knowledge disparity, along with a new dataset and methodology that can be adapted to assess progress in any field or time period. Our results on economics, politics, and the search for extraterrestrial intelligence (SETI) demonstrate that a surge in productivity often precedes significant advancements, while also revealing unexpected knowledge gaps that offer new research opportunities and underscore the importance of transparent evaluation metrics in complex studies. Our study paves the way for a more nuanced understanding of scientific progress, pinpointing areas where further efforts may yield substantial dividends and highlighting the value of rigorous evaluation in critical investigations. One significant limitation of existing text-based games lies in their slow speed, topping out at around 100 actions per second, largely because of outdated technology used to create them.
Our research presents TextWorldExpress, a highly optimized version of three widely used text-based game challenges, achieving a remarkable increase in simulation processing speed of roughly three orders of magnitude.
On ordinary computer hardware, it can process over one million actions per second, allowing for extensive tests lasting merely a day rather than weeks or even months. As a result, researchers can conduct a larger number of iterations in a limited amount of time, making it easier to detect subtle differences between various virtual agent approaches. We show that the simplified interface of TextWorldExpress slightly reduces the difficulties encountered by virtual agents in comparison to the original games, but demonstrate that this reduction is minimal and largely confined to very easy levels, by performing a detailed analysis of multiple evaluation metrics. TextWorldExpress is available online for public access, providing a highly advanced benchmark for evaluating the performance of virtual agents in text-based games. We invite other researchers to contribute their own text-based games simulated within this same framework, which can be easily integrated into our existing system, further expanding the range of topics that virtual agents need to be able to handle. We have accomplished this improvement by replacing the outdated technology used to create these games with more efficient, modern approaches, allowing multiple actions to be processed simultaneously, and fine-tuning the system performance, resulting in significant performance gains without compromising the level of difficulty or other essential characteristics of these games. We believe that our research will provide valuable insights to numerous other fields of research that rely on simulated environments, and we hope that our results will motivate other researchers to follow a similar path in optimizing their own research tools. We have followed this approach to optimize three widely used text-based games, resulting in a significant increase in simulation processing speed of over a million times, allowing for extensive tests to be conducted in a day rather than weeks or even months. This has become possible because of the recent advancement in modern Python frameworks, allowing transcriptions of the game environment to be updated simultaneously, and our expertise in creating complex virtual worlds using Python, which has been successfully demonstrated in our research. We have created TextWorldExpress, a highly advanced virtual golf game, called Minigolf, a highly challenging virtual escape room, called Exit and a highly intricate virtual fiction, called FrickAndFang

This paper presents an optimized LSTM design for video identification that combines algorithmic and hardware advancements. In the proposed algorithmic approach, the LSTM model is transformed into a more efficient form using the Hierarchical Tucker (HT) tensor decomposition technique. This optimization reduces model parameters by 95% compared to the original LSTM. To facilitate efficient computation on the decomposed model, a custom hardware design called the Tensor Decomposition Accelerator (TDA) is developed. The TDA features a hierarchical data path that mimics the decomposed tensor structure, enabling fast matrix-vector operations with minimal data migration. Key TDA components include a Spatial Decomposition Path (SDP) that handles fine-grained tensor subblocks and a Temporal Decomposition Path (TDP) that manages coarser subblocks. The TDA's unique architecture offers enhanced energy efficiency and performance compared to standard digital signal processor-based approaches. In video identification applications, the proposed LSTM network exhibits superior accuracy and outperforms existing deep learning models. Furthermore, the TDA implementation demonstrates substantial energy savings and offers a high performance-to-area ratio, making it an energy-efficient hardware solution. The TDA's effectiveness is validated across multiple video identification datasets, and the research provides a viable path for the practical application of deep learning models in resource-constrained systems. Significant advancements in NLP have been observed in the last few years, thanks largely to large-scale supervised learning techniques and vast amounts of publicly available data. However, there are still numerous NLP applications where data is limited, hindering the scale and diversity necessary for successful model deployment. Human-annotated data is scarce, yet existing datasets are often insufficient due to their limited size. As a result, augmenting existing datasets without increasing the reliance on human-annotated data is crucial for further breakthroughs in NLP under low-data conditions. Various data augmentation techniques have been tried with different models and tasks but a clear, comprehensive understanding of their effectiveness remains elusive. In this study, we examine multiple data augmentation methods thoroughly in low-resource NLP settings, considering both few-shot and zero-shot scenarios, with emphasis on transparent, reproducible experiments. Our findings provide valuable insights into the performance of distinct models, techniques, and setups, showcasing the relative merits of different augmentation methods, model configurations, and latency requirements. Ultimately, our study serves as a starting point for future research into more innovative data augmentation techniques and other methods for enhancing model performance under low-data conditions. This benchmark is available for public use at https://github.com/paper-benchmarks/Tabert14-benchmark. Our study has also been incorporated into a longer technical report that is available for review at https://arxiv.org/abs/2109.02121. Both the benchmark and the extended report can be used as reference points for the community. The concept of a semi-dilute phase in polymer solutions has been reexamined in the context of a gravitational system, with the semi-dilute phase corresponding to a non-linear regime of polymer interactions. We argue that cross-linking polymers acts as a model for charged operators in conformal field theories, and following this analogy, we prove the convexity of these operators. This result is relevant to the "feeble gravity" conjecture, which would imply that the semi-dilute phase of a gravitational system is closer to the linear regime than the polymer model alone, and we use our proof to provide a subset of counterfactual evidence for this conjecture. Additionally, our discussion includes an exploration of relationships between polymer models, conformal field theories, and gravitational systems in higher dimensions. The convexity of these operators is confirmed through a direct analysis of the polymer model's free energy, with the outcome supported by numerous theoretical frameworks including the gravitational central charge, holographic duality, and mean-field approximations. The underlying reasons for the convexity of charged operators are found to stem from a combination of the negative central charge of Liouville field theory and the gravitational interaction, which together reduce the curvature of the operator spectrum. The feeble gravity conjecture is proposed to have a broader application to the global geometry of gravitational system phases, with implications for the possibility of first-order phase transitions. The proposed feeble gravity conjecture has been earlier linked to the idea that gravitational systems may only exhibit second-order phase transitions, and our results further establish that this relationship holds true in the semi-dilute polymer regime. The convexity of charged operators is demonstrated to result in a reduction in the magnitude of the discrepancy between the gravitational system's behavior and the predictions of mean-field theories, and potentially holds the key to understanding why gravitational systems may only undergo second-order phase transitions. The relationship between polymer models, conformal field theories, and gravitational systems suggests that the proposed feeble gravity conjecture could be tested through experiments involving the dissolution of polymers in gravitational systems, and our analysis provides a framework for the development of a more comprehensive theory of gravitational phase transitions that incorporates both classical and quantum gravitational forces. The convexity of charged operators is shown to be a key factor influencing the behavior of gravitational systems in the semi-dilute phase, and this conclusion is supported by numerous theoretical frameworks. Critical infrastructure, essential for a city's functioning and stability, is often maintained by companies that provide complementary services to key industries, such as data centers, power plants, or transportation hubs. The escalating demand for these services, driven by increasing digitalization and interconnection, creates opportunities for companies to exploit market power and restrict competition in the delivery of essential infrastructure services. To address these concerns, policymakers seek innovative strategies, such as subsidies, tax incentives, or regulated service portfolios, to promote competition and accessibility in the auxiliary services market. However, the complex interplay between companies, consumers, and the broader market context makes it challenging to evaluate the effectiveness of these policies. To overcome this limitation, we introduce a novel model that uses game theory to analyze the behavior of companies in a dynamic market and incorporates the effects of policy interventions. By drawing on studies of network economics and urban development, we leverage the model to investigate the impact of policy decisions on competition, pricing, and service quality in the auxiliary services market. Our research framework is applicable to multiple types of companies and can be tailored to address specific policy concerns, such as promoting competition or service quality through pricing regulations or subsidies. We demonstrate the practical utility of our model by exploring its implications for companies, consumers, and the broader market in response to different policy interventions. Furthermore, our research raises intriguing questions about the interplay between companies and the underlying urban network, presenting an opportunity for future research to build upon our model and further explore these dynamics. By doing so, we can develop a more comprehensive understanding of the urban economy, as well as the potential for urban networks to influence company behavior and market outcomes. This integrated perspective can provide valuable insights for policymakers seeking to create effective policies that address the complexities of urban economics and network effects. We showcase the model's applicability to the critical infrastructure services market, but it can be adapted to other contexts, such as the cybersecurity industry. Our model highlights the significance of considering the urban network's effects on company behavior and market interactions in the auxiliary services market. It also demonstrates the limited effectiveness of traditional policy approaches, such as regulating company behavior or network architecture. Instead, targeting the underlying urban network through infrastructure investments or urban planning can yield more significant benefits in terms of increased competition, lower prices, and improved service quality. We investigate the potential of future $e^+e^-$ colliders, specifically at 250 GeV and 1 TeV, to study a beyond Standard Model scenario where a scalar multiplet is expanded and a light Higgs boson exists. We focus on the production processes of $Zh$ and $h\gamma$. In this theoretical framework, we develop general expressions for the observables of these processes and derive optimal bounds on the model parameters based on projected sensitivities of these processes at the two collider energies. We discover that in the case of $h\gamma$ at 250 GeV, the optimal bound on the new scalar mass is around 350 GeV, while in the case of $Zh$ at 1 TeV, the optimal bound on the new scalar mass is around 800 GeV. We find that in the most favorable scenario, where all new scalars are nearly degenerate and their primary production mode is through a chain decay to Higgs bosons, the optimal bounds on the new scalar mass can be as low as 280 GeV for $h\gamma$ at 250 GeV and 1.3 TeV for $Zh$ at 1 TeV. We also observe that in the scenario where the light Higgs boson has a significant coupling to heavy quarks, the optimal bounds on the new scalar mass can be as low as 330 GeV for $h\gamma$ at 250 GeV and 1.5 TeV for $Zh$ at 1 TeV. Additionally, we find that in the scenario where the light Higgs boson has a significant coupling to gauge bosons, the optimal bounds on the new scalar mass can be as low as 340 GeV for $h\gamma$ at 250 GeV and 1.4 TeV for $Zh$ at 1 TeV. We also derive the optimal bounds on the Higgs boson coupling modifiers and observe that in the most favorable scenario, the optimal bound on the $Zh$ production cross-section can be as low as 0.06 fb, and the optimal bound on the $h\gamma$ branching ratio can be as low as $0.10\%$. Resonant x-ray scattering in the nuclear range offers a promising new method for investigating the interplay between electronic and nuclear degrees of freedom and provides a means to write quantum information into nuclear levels using x-ray light, which can then be stored and retrieved through scattering scans at specific resonances. This new technique surpasses the limitations of scattering by incorporating propagation of x-ray photons, x-ray-light induced changes in the local potential, and the scattering of x-rays by electrons and nuclei, and holds potential for diverse applications such as quantum data storage and the precise measurement of nuclear magnetic moment. We introduce a novel mixed finite element method that combines elements of both standard and non-conforming methods for solving single-phase Darcy flow in massive fractures. Our approach uses non-conforming triangular finite elements in the fracture to capture the higher conductivity of the fracture, while employing a more refined grid in the bulk domain. This method is mathematically equivalent to a mixed finite element method using piecewise constant functions in the bulk and piecewise polynomial functions in the fracture. This approach offers an alternative to previous methods, such as standard mixed finite element and boundary element methods, and our analysis confirms that our method preserves the same a priori error bounds as these methods, despite using a coarser grid in the fracture. This method is implemented and its performance is compared with the boundary element method, showing similar performance but better scalability. This method is an attractive option for simulations involving large fractures, providing an efficient and accurate approach for modeling such flows. This work also highlights potential applications to multi-phase flow and transport in fractured porous media. The explosive synchronization phenomenon occurs when a population of oscillators transitions from a disordered state to a synchronized one in a single, abrupt event. A graph's edge coloring can be described as assigning different colors to each edge so that no two adjacent edges have the same color, and this concept has been extensively explored in relation to other characteristics of a graph. Notably, a long-standing conjecture states that a graph with a specific property - being bipartite and having a chromatic number equal to half the number of vertices - can be colored using half the number of possible colors. A recent proof supported this conjecture, but it has now been shown that this proof contains a flaw and does not hold true for a specific type of bipartite graph. A particular type of bipartite graph with specific properties - being planar, simple, and triply connected - was previously demonstrated to have a proof for the half-color conjecture in a relatively short number of pages. However, a new finding presents a different type of bipartite graph that is also planar, simple, and triply connected but fails the condition of being publicly known, indicating that its structure is not fully understood. When comparing this new discovery to the previous proven instance, it was found that the previous proof's approach can be applied generally to all cubic bipartite graphs with a chromatic number of four, except possibly those with a structure similar to the new discovery. Convolutional neural networks are integral to various safety-critical computer vision applications like human robot interaction and self-driving technology. Real-world deployments of these systems require ensuring the reliability of their underlying hardware, as unexpected errors can compromise performance and safety. For instance, a mistake in a pixel coordinate calculation could lead to a buffer overflow, allowing malicious memory access and system instability. To address this issue, we propose a technique called activation range supervision, which tracks neural network activity across all layers to prevent excessive input values from entering subsequent layers. However, implementing this approach requires significant changes to the code, particularly for pre-trained models and legacy systems. To overcome this limitation, we developed a patent-pending method to incorporate our supervision technique into neural networks through code obfuscation, achieving similar error reduction and activation value containment results. Our technique was successfully tested on a range of convolutional neural networks, and the obtained data suggests our approach can efficiently detect a variety of errors, including fault injection scenarios. The performance of our method also shows minimal precision degradation and comparable latency increases to other error detection methods, while successfully containing activation values within desired ranges. The implemented system we evaluated consists of a Google Coral Camera and a Raspberry Pi 4 computer, and the code for our method is available online. Furthermore, our study includes a safety case analysis, and the document provides a comprehensive overview of the developed system, safety case analysis, and experimental results.

These measurements are made possible by the combined use of the ALICE detector's central detector system and the ALICE Forward Multiplicity Detector. A distinct feature of these measurements is the use of an invariant yield instead of the differential cross-section, which allows for a better interpretation of data in context with other collisions systems. These measurements span a range of transverse momenta from 0.3 to 5.0 GeV/$c$ and are relevant for further studies of particle production and nuclear force parameters. Moreover, a comparison with 5.02 TeV Pb-Pb data reveals a trend of increased particle production in more central collisions, and a ratio of $p_{\rm T}$-integrated yields displaying dependencies on transverse momentum. Additionally, a comparison with 2.76 TeV Pb-Pb data shows particle production increasing with larger transverse momenta in more central collisions. In late October 2019, nationwide protests erupted in Chile, leading to severe consequences including prolonged civilian-military confrontations and the implementation of strict curfews. A significant factor contributing to these events was the sudden and drastic reduction of fuel prices, which had an unexpected reverse effect on the public. To provide a theoretical framework for understanding these events, we developed an epidemiological non-local model incorporating geographical distance and temporary immune response effects. Our model reveals the emergence of complex dynamics, notably including a critical value for the temporary immunity's impact, which influences disease equilibrium solutions. Furthermore, we verify the model's analytical solutions numerically and graphically, and explore its implications in the context of the Chilean protests. Finally, we highlight key policy recommendations derived from our model's predictions. Additionally, we discuss potential extensions to our model, including the inclusion of government intervention and temporary immunity response in a more complex multi-layer network. This study presents an innovative approach to analyzing complex real-world phenomena through mathematical modeling. The model's insights offer valuable implications for epidemiological models, while also highlighting the utility of non-epidemiological systems being analyzed through epidemiological models. This study demonstrates the beneficial outcome of this approach, which can be applied to a broad range of real-world scenarios. The associated code can be found at: https://github.com/rodrigomartino/Chilean-Protests-Model. The model's results have been presented at the 2020 ENSI (Encontres de Physique de Particules) conference and the 2022 (virtual) UMAM (Universidade do Minho) conference. The model's analysis has significant bearing on current global events, such as the 2022 Ukrainian protests following the invasion of Ukraine. This model is currently being adapted to analyze the impact of temperature on disease dynamics. The model's key feature, temporary immunity, is being replaced by a driver that follows an exponential distribution, given that Chile's Department of Health uses this approach to model fuel price's impact on the protests. The adapted model is now being used to analyze the recent 2023 heatwave in Europe, particularly the excessive heat in the French city of Marseilles. The model is also being applied to study the impact of population migration on the transmission of infectious diseases, with a specific case study on the recent COVID-19 outbreak in the city of Curitiba, Brazil. We examined the relationship between star formation rates (SFRs) in the Local Universe, determined through observation of the Brackett-$\gamma$ (BL$\gamma$) line and by fitting spectral energy distribution (SEDs). Our results show that SFRs from BL$\gamma$ and SEDs are highly correlated ($\sigma_{\textrm{ratio}}=0.20$) with a mean ratio of 0.84, indicating that SFRs from these methods are comparable. However, SFRs from BL$\gamma$ are generally higher than those from SEDs due to the latter's systematic underestimation, likely caused by dust heating from post-Asympototic Giant Branch stars and supernovae. We found that SED fitting's assumption of a top-light initial mass function may also contribute to this underestimation. Notably, SFRs from both methods follow the same scaling with gas mass fraction. Our study highlights the value of using a gold-standard method like BL$\gamma$ to evaluate the performance of SED fitting across a broad range of galaxy populations. Furthermore, it suggests that the intrinsic scatter in the far-ULIRG regime's starburst sequence may be as small as $\sigma_{\textrm{ratio}}}=0.20$.$\square$ We suggest modifying the 24$\mu$m PET method to incorporate SFRs from SEDs that consider the underestimation mentioned above. Additionally, due to the underestimation of SFRs from SEDs, the starburst sequence's scatter might be greater than previously reported. We introduce a novel class of materials, which we call square-root higher-order Weyl materials, where a crucial parameter is reduced by half in both spatial and momentum dimensions. This class exhibits exceptional properties when their energy spectrum near Weyl points is analyzed, where a revised higher-order Weyl phenomenon occurs. As a result, these materials can display anomalous Hall responses that are significantly enhanced, reaching an unprecedented level equivalent to the cyclotron mass. Furthermore, their universal magnetic field dependence arises from a unique combination of all possible combinations of spatial and momentum separations of electric field components. This leads to a critical field value, below which the anomalous Nernst effect can be explained by the standard Fermi-liquid theory, but we show that this value can be manipulated by adjusting key parameters of these materials. Our proposed framework offers a practical means to design these materials, potentially enabling the creation of devices that can simultaneously achieve high carrier velocities and long carrier lifetimes. Our theoretical predictions can be experimentally validated through measurements of the specific heat, anomalous Nernst coefficient, and transverse magnetization. Our study provides a foundational understanding of square-root higher-order Weyl materials and suggests potential paths for their technological application. This paper delves into the vertex operator algebra structure of the parafermion type, in association with highest weight modules for integrable representations of the superalgebra $osp(1|2n)$, a simple affine Lie superalgebra. We establish the underlying generators of this algebra in detail. Moreover, we identify a specific condition on the level $k$ for the vertex operator algebra to be rational. Furthermore, we determine the indecomposability of this vertex operator algebra when $k$ satisfies this condition. Additionally, we establish isomorphisms between $K(osp(1|2n),k)$ and certain lattice vertex operator algebras, specifically the extended $A_{2n-1}(1)_{k}$ lattice vertex operator algebras, for levels $k$ that are integers greater than 0. This relationship holds for both fermionic and bosonic cases. We explore this connection by relating the underlying modules of $osp(1|2n)$ to twisted modules of the affine Lie (super)algebra $sl(2n|kn)$. This correspondence establishes a connection between the roots of the vertex operator algebra and the central extension of the algebra. It demonstrates that the level $k$ of the vertex operator algebra represents the level of the twisted module rather than the central charge of the vertex operator algebra. This insight provides a clear explanation for the phenomenon observed in $A_{2n-1}$, where the condition for $k$ to be an integer greater than 0 is for the resulting vertex operator algebra to be rational. This relationship also sheds light on the indecomposability of $K(osp(1|2n),k)$ by considering the twisted module of $sl(2n|kn)$, which is a module of type I. It is therefore indecomposable. It is also shown that $K(osp(1|2n),k)$ contains a module of type I, which follows from this relationship and the properties of twisted modules of simple affine Lie superalgebras. This connection also provides evidence that the vertex operator algebra $K(osp(1|2n),k)$ is isomorphic to a type I module, which is consistent with previous findings. This relationship holds for both fermionic and bosonic cases. It is also demonstrated that $K(osp(1|2n),k)$ contains a module of type I, which follows from this relationship and the properties of twisted modules of simple affine Lie superalgebras.

Approximately a decade ago, researchers proposed the grid cell hypothesis, suggesting that a specific network in the medial temporal lobe is responsible for generating periodic spatial representations. These proposed grid systems have been modeled in various contexts using intrinsically stable periodic waves in three-dimensional networks of neurons with excitatory and inhibitory connections. While our initial understanding of grid cells came from model predictions, recent discoveries of grid cells in animals and humans through neuroimaging have validated these concepts. As a result, the focus has shifted from confirming the existence of grid cells to analyzing the underlying neural mechanisms that produce these periodic representations. This survey examines recent advancements in modeling grid cell behavior, emphasizing studies of the 3D entorhinal grid network, as well as related applications of neural population dynamics and control. We discuss current limitations of these models, common themes in the underlying mechanisms, and future research directions motivated by our findings. Additionally, we provide an open-source framework for simulating these neural systems, enabling flexible exploration of their underlying mechanics. As our understanding of brain function continues to evolve, so too will our models of grid cell behavior. Thus, it is essential to acknowledge the limitations of our current approaches and to emerge with a more cohesive theoretical foundation. This includes the potential for higher-level concepts, such as brain network control and the dual roles of the hippocampus, to further advance our knowledge of neural systems. Finally, we conclude by highlighting the broader implications of grid cell research for our understanding of other periodic phenomena in the brain. This includes the potential for grid cell models to contribute to a broader theory of neural oscillations, as well as the importance of distinguishing between different types of periodic behavior, such as stable fixed points, and those that are dynamically maintained by the interplay between competing forces. This study explores the impact of differential rotation in low-rotating solar-type stars on global magnetic activity in their convection zones. We developed three all-numerical models representing possible rotation patterns: pro-solar, anti-solar, and intermediate differential rotation scenarios. The anti-solar scenario, characterized by a rotation rate decreasing with latitude, was specifically investigated in this research. We discovered that this rotation pattern disrupts the generation of magnetic multipoles, thereby hindering the creation of toroidal magnetic fields through the differential rotation process. As a result, only poloidal magnetic fields generated by the $\alpha$-effect can be present in these stars. Furthermore, we found that increasing the generation of the $\alpha$-effect by 10% can compensate for the inhibition of toroidal field generation, leading to the creation of both poloidal and toroidal magnetic fields. This increased $\alpha$-effect generation can be achieved under high magnetic filling factors or in stars with enhanced turbulent buoyancy. Additionally, we observed that the possibility of magnetic cycles in these stars depends on several factors, including their rotational period, magnetic energy, and the generated magnetic flux. We found that only stars with generated magnetic flux below a certain threshold can exhibit magnetic cycles. We also discovered that the possibility of magnetic cycles decreases with increasing rotational period, magnetic energy, and generated magnetic flux. Lastly, we found that stars with downflows dominating their convective flows can experience magnetic cycles, whereas stars with upflows dominating their convective flows cannot. This research provides new insights that can be utilized in the development of whole-star magneto-hydrodynamic models, incorporating various rotation patterns, and these findings can be applied to a wide range of low-rotating solar-type stars. Additionally, these results can offer explanations for the magnetic behavior in stars like the Sun, as well as in stars exhibiting odd parity magnetic field patterns, such as $\tau$ Pav. Moreover, these findings imply that the presence of magnetic cycles in these stars depends on their magnetic energy, generated magnetic flux, rotational period, and convective flow patterns. Ultimately, this research highlights the importance of considering different rotation patterns in the magnetic behavior of low-rotating solar-type stars. Lastly, we provide several predictions and observational tests that can be conducted to further validate these theoretical models. These predictions include analyzing stars with generated magnetic flux below the solar level, comparing the magnetic energy and generated magnetic flux of slow and fast rotating stars with similar convective energy, as well as observing stars with downflows dominating their convective flows.

A new class of holographic surges in Vasiliev's gravity has been discovered at the interface between two conformal field theory regions, and this phenomenon exhibits rushed QNEC behavior.  The rushed QNEC generates an accelerated differential growth of entanglement length (ΔL_E) in proportion to the ADE Lie algebras, and its fundamental rush rate is constant across all surges and bounds, and is determined by the speed of causal propagation.  The rush rate of decoherence, represented by the standard Komar mass, is instead tied to the quadratic growth of entanglement, and results in the emergence of bound states that maintain stationary entanglement networks.  The rush rate of decoherence can be slowed down with a negative dark mass, allowing for the creation of superluminal bound states of particles, and the preservation of stationary entanglement networks requires the satisfaction of the Strong Holographic Principle.  The rush rate of state vector growth exceeds the particle production rate from a collapsing black hole, and contributes to the formation of gravitational waves, and the rush rate of decoherence leads to the issue of whether gravitational waves carry entanglement information, and the resulting conclusion that this information is spread over the stationary entanglement network. Superconducting quantum circuits are emerging as prominent platforms for quantum computing. For practical applications, it is essential to address material flaws causing decoherence. This study employs terahertz Scanning Near-field Optical Microscopy to analyze the local dielectric characteristics and carrier concentrations in aluminum resonators on silicon substrates, critical components of superconducting quantum processors. Utilizing a vector calibration method, we determined the terahertz permittivity near the microwave feedline and found that etched silicon exhibits higher carrier concentrations than oxide etched silicon. We further investigate methods to reduce carrier concentrations, demonstrating the utility of near-field terahertz investigations in evaluating and identifying loss channels in quantum devices. Additionally, we explore methods to enhance the spectral response of probe systems, incorporating a new strategy using a co-planar probe design. This approach boosts the signal-to-noise ratio and allows for the non-invasive assessment of resonance modes within the silicon substrate. We demonstrate our technique's effectiveness on various resonators, including those fabricated with niobium and gold. Further advancements in this technique hold the potential to monitor carrier concentrations, resistivity, and mechanical defects within quantum devices. This study is an early contribution to the investigation of quantum devices using near-field terahertz methods, a field that this research group is leading in collaboration with J.Q. You. This workshop brings together scientists working on the atmosphere of Venus, to share recent findings and discuss future research opportunities to better understand the planet's atmosphere. Venus, despite being Earth-like in size and composition, has an extremely hostile environment due to its thick CO2-rich atmosphere, resulting in surface temperatures and pressures that are hostile to most life forms. Understanding the past development of Venus is crucial, as it can provide insights into the evolution of Earth and other terrestrial planets. The atmosphere of Venus has developed over a billion years through interactions between the sun, surface processes, and geological and geophysical processes. Water steam, the primary volatile on Venus, has undergone extensive cycling throughout the planet's history, ultimately leading to the present composition of acidic carbon dioxide. Volcanic activity has played a key role in exchanging gases between the surface, crust, and atmosphere. The surface of Venus is home to vast plains formed from volcanic eruptions and tectonic activity, while massive old volcanoes have been reshaped by extensive fluidized flow. Evidence of tectonic activity, impact craters, and the planet's Yarkovsky effect constrain Venus's accretion history and its early formation period. Venus orbits the sun closest, affecting its climate and orbital path. Orbital variations have caused temperature fluctuations and changes in the atmosphere's mass, while a supergreenhouse effect has maintained a stable temperature difference between the day and night sides of the planet. Observations of Venus are crucial for studying the planet's interior, geology, and geophysics. Ground and space-based missions such as NASA's DAVINCHI, NASA's VERITAS, NASA's DASE, and the ESA's SHARAD have contributed significantly to our understanding of Venus. Rank metric encryption was initially proposed by Kassab and Cousinou in 2001, and it reaches a security level comparable to that of lattice-based cryptography, without relying on error-prone decimal arithmetic. A major obstacle in implementing rank metric encryption methods is the lack of an efficient decoding algorithm for integer matrices. While Gaussian decoding has been shown to be effective in various applications, its effectiveness decreases significantly when the matrix is highly symmetric and has low rank. In this research, we introduce a novel decoding approach that leverages the matrix's symmetric properties and geometric features of its null space, and we prove the algorithm's optimal performance when the matrix has specific symmetry characteristics. Our results demonstrate a significant improvement over conventional decoding methods, especially for small ranks, and we showcase the algorithm's practical utility through an secure code construction example. Additionally, this research raises intriguing theoretical questions and sets a new benchmark for future decoding algorithm developments. We also explore potential connections between our decoding method and other mathematical concepts, such as monoid decomposition and lattice reduction, and we anticipate these connections to spark further research in the field. While our proposed algorithm outperforms Gaussian decoding for low-rank matrices, we suspect that its actual improvement could be even greater than what is statistically measurable, and we hope this paper will inspire others to experiment with this hypothesis. We have made our algorithm publicly available for others to test and evaluate. To understand the structure of dark matter, a deep learning framework has been implemented and used to explore the significance of the cosmic speed field in forming halo masses. The study leverages a widely accepted paradigm, where the cosmic web affects matter distribution, and employs a physics-informed neural network to mimic the relationship between the cosmic speed field and halo masses. The analysis reveals that the neural network's predictions for halo masses are remarkably consistent with observations, indicating that the model has effectively captured the underlying processes. However, removing the cosmic speed field's influence and relying solely on the physics-informed neural network's knowledge, results in a significant discrepancy in the predicted halo masses when compared to observations, suggesting that the cosmic speed field plays a crucial role in the formation of halo masses. To reconcile this, the model is modified to include a random factor, which yields a good match with observations, implying that the cosmic speed field is not sufficient on its own and that other processes also contribute to the formation of halo masses. The study demonstrates the powerful capability of deep learning techniques in analyzing complex cosmological phenomena and sheds light on the intricate relationship between the cosmic speed field and halo masses. The implementation of these techniques may also be a suitable approach for investigating other fundamental processes in the formation of dark matter halos. The study's findings contribute to the ongoing discussion in the scientific community and could pave the way for further research into the complex relationships governing the formation of dark matter halos. The proposed framework can be applied to an unprecedented number of simulation outputs, which includes a highly detailed $21$ billion light-year-scale simulation, and showcases the feasibility of using deep learning to explore the nature of cosmological simulations on an unprecedented scale. The study's results may be of interest to the broader scientific community involved in the investigation of dark matter and dark energy, and the ongoing quest to understand the universe's fundamental properties. The knowledge gained from the study could be used to direct ongoing and future observations, and the proposed deep learning framework can be used to explore the underlying processes of cosmological simulations, which may also be applicable to other research fields. Automatically processing these recordings is crucial for making historical performances accessible via video sharing platforms and facilitating the discovery of hidden treasures in archival collections.  A method has been developed to accurately transcribe recordings of these instruments using only a partial set of labeled recordings.  First, the proposed method performs low-rank factorization of the recorded sound while minimizing noise, then uses Neighbor Embedding Constrained Nonnegative Matrix Factorization to ensure that factorized components match the characteristics of labeled data. Comprehensive tests demonstrate that this method surpasses existing semi-supervised techniques.  The proposed method also successfully transcribes recordings of various sound sources while reducing the required labeled data by half. This method, tailored for quasi-static evolution applications, utilizes a Lagrangian formulation where fluid elements are located by solving balance equations, in contrast to the conventional Eulerian method. This innovative approach eschews the use of the Euler equation's first integral, often obtained analytically under simplifying conditions, in favor of assigning unique properties to each fluid element. This includes individual masses, specific angular momentum, and entropy levels. 

As a key departure from earlier methodologies, the angular velocity distribution within each fluid element is instead determined after the positions of all elements are calculated, allowing for more nuanced configurations. This method involves solving a vast set of nonlinear algebraic equations derived from time-independent versions of the Euler and Einstein equations, solved through our new multi-dimensional root-finding algorithm, the W4 method.

This study is centered on a key finding from a prior paper by J. A. Galtier, which discovered that certain locomotion patterns maintained optimal speed and efficiency during rapid, irregular fluid fluctuations. To further explore this concept, our research enhances previous models by incorporating a more comprehensive "benthic" model that accounts for a swimmer's internal organs and presents two case studies on the optimal swimmer body plan. One case considers a swimmer moving in a fluid with limited boundary layer restrictions, while the other examines a swimmer operating in a fluid where internal organ impact is significant. Both case studies reveal that the optimal swimmer body plan reduces symmetry and achieves a more asymmetrical shape than the benthic model would suggest. Additionally, our results indicate that forcing the swimmer to maintain a symmetrical shape results in lower optimal speed gains. Notably, the benthic model is validated by experimental data on the scallop, a marine animal that loses mobility when its muscles become non-functional. However, surprisingly, even in such circumstances, the optimal body plan continues to provide a significant advantage in movement efficiency. This insight may offer a clue to the evolutionary origins of the scallop's body structure. To manually replicate the optimal swimmer body plan without the benefit of computational tools, we outline a step-by-step procedure involving successive refinements of the swimmer's shape in a series of two-dimensional fluid dynamics simulations. A key innovation of our research is the introduction of a novel measure for swimmer elasticity that correlates with the broad features of its body plan. Building on previous work by Galtier, our study identifies distinct typical behaviors for swimmers with either short or long stalks. Notably, the former exhibit strong resistance to large amplitude fluctuations and show little improvement in speed optimization through the optimal body plan, whereas the latter demonstrate a significant increase in speed when the swimmer's shape is matched to the fluid's boundary layer. Furthermore, our study finds that in cases where the fluid boundary layer restricts swimmer movement, the optimal body plan results in a 25% increase in speed, whereas this benefit drops to around 10% when movement is no longer restricted. Interestingly, even in scenarios where the swimmer is forced to maintain a symmetrical shape, the optimal body plan continues to provide a significant speed gain, indicating that this strategy is advantageous across various elastic swimmer configurations. Additionally, our results show that forcing the swimmer to have an irregular shape does not result in a corresponding increase in speed when the fluid boundary layer is unrestricted.

Massive protostars, depending on their age, have either already reached their final mass or will eventually return a significant portion of their current mass to their surrounding environment.  This process is largely influenced by the transitions of massive stars from high to low mass, which occur when nuclear reactions slow down, as well as the mergers of binary and multiple star systems.  In this study, we examine how the growth of massive protostars is shaped by the accretion of material broken up by the disruption of nearby star formation, as well as the direct addition of solid and gas components from the dissolution of massive star systems.  By exploring the possible laboratory conditions of massive protostars and considering constraints from observations and theoretical models of massive star formation and binary interactions, we develop a useable set of models that cover the evolution of massive protostars across a wide range of masses.  Our theoretical models suggest that massive protostars generally reach nuclear equilibrium in a short period of time, and then continue to grow at a slower rate until their surrounding disks are depleted.  From then on, the mass of the star becomes fixed, with any additional material accumulating in the form of solid particles.  This leads to a greater abundance of dust in the surroundings of more massive protostars.  Our findings also predict specific spectral features for the most massive protostars, which involve a mix of broad hydrogen emission lines and a forest of weaker lines due to the accumulation of metal-rich gas that is being ejected at a high velocity. The theory of contest equations has been a significant area of study in economics and mathematics for some time, and has applications in biology as well. Contests can be understood through the lens of group theory, and models based on totally ordered groups offer valuable insights, despite being less well-known than their abelian counterparts. This paper makes an initial foray into the realm of totally ordered groups in the context of contests, and proves that equilibriums in one-dimensional contests result in outcomes that are directly proportional to the degree of a polynomial associated with each player's strategy. A model of repeated contests, modelled as a finite number of independent identically distributed random variables, is also considered and shows that the rule of proportionality can be an equilibrium strategy under specific conditions. The subclass of magnetic Cataclysmic Variables, asynchronous polars, still lacks a comprehensive understanding. Asynchronous polars are a category of polars characterized by their white dwarf spin period differing significantly, whether longer or shorter, from their binary orbital period. The detection rate of asynchronous polars in soft gamma-ray observations is disproportionate, implying that they might naturally have more intense X-ray spectra. In order to explore the link between a Cataclysmic Variable's synchronization status and its X-ray hardness ratio, we conducted a comparison between standard and asynchronous polars using their entire sample set from the MAXI telescope over ten years. Our statistical analysis indicates that a Cataclysmic Variable's synchronization status is associated with its X-ray hardness ratio. No difference was found in the hardness ratios of standard and non-standard asynchronous polars, indicating that the greater hardness ratio seen in asynchronous polars isn't linked to the spin period relationship between the two components. Instead, it may be caused by accretion stream impact on the non-synchronized pole of the binary system. In cases where the secondary star's heating dominates the binary system's behavior, this would result in a lower density accretion disk and hence a harder X-ray spectrum. Moreover, we found that standard and non-standard polars exhibit the same spectral characteristics, supporting the idea that the absence of detected non-standard polars in hard gamma-ray observations might be a detection bias rather than a real phenomenon. Finally, we suggest that X-ray telescopes with higher sensitivity, such as those on board X-ray telescopes like XMM-Newton and Chandra, be utilized for further studies of this kind. Doing so could provide greater insight into the unique characteristics of asynchronous polars and their relationship with standard polars. Additionally, we propose that binary systems with observed extreme X-ray hardness ratios could be identified as potential members of the asynchronous polars subgroup. FourierMask uses a Fourier transformation on the coordinate positions and feeds the mapped features to an implicit function represented by a coordinate-based multi-layer perceptron (MLP). This enables FourierMask to predict specific instance masks and adapt the Fourier transformation for various objects, thus making it applicable to real-world image instances. Since implicit functions operate seamlessly over the input domain, FourierMask can generate higher-resolution masks with fewer input pixel coordinates. By integrating a renderer MLP (FourierRend), we demonstrate significant enhancements to mask quality using the predictions of FourierMask. Compared to Mask R-CNN at the same resolution, FourierMask achieves comparable performance on the MS COCO dataset while delivering superior results at higher resolutions. Additionally, FourierMask exhibits superior performance to implicit mask prediction methods while being computationally efficient. The code is publicly available at https://github.com/ruotianeng/fourier-mask.

Skin cancer can be extremely deadly if left untreated, and early detection is crucial for its survival rate.  Image recognition technology has the potential to be a game-changer in dermatology by raising the accuracy of cancer diagnosis and reducing the risk associated with long waits for expert opinions.  To achieve this, we propose a novel approach that combines a non-local total variation model with maximum likelihood estimation to remove the noise in dermoscopy images, followed by an entropy-based outlier detection method using local intrinsic dimensionality.  This approach allows the system to identify unusual images that may indicate cancer by determining the entropy of each image, based on the distribution of its features.  We demonstrated the effectiveness of this approach by applying it to a dermoscopy image dataset, and the results show that it can be up to 20% more accurate in detecting cancer than existing methods.  However, further research is needed to validate these results across multiple datasets.  We also discovered that reducing the outlier detection threshold can increase the accuracy of cancer detection, but this may compromise the system's ability to detect all cancers.  Overall, this study lays the groundwork for the development of highly reliable, low-risk skin cancer detection systems. Researchers propose that this similarity might reflect a reaction pathway that involves the transfer of a hydrogen atom. In neural machine translation, the focus of the attention model plays a crucial role in determining phrases to focus on in the source language and translate them into the target language. However, current attention models can struggle with ordering and cannot consider future elements of the sentence. This research introduces an innovative attention model with look-ahead focus, capable of breaking down the translation task into multiple segments and reusing previous and future contextual information to improve performance. Our experiments demonstrate substantial gains from this approach, particularly in translating lengthy sentences and improving grammatical accuracy. Our method also significantly reduces the computational requirements compared to traditional attention models. We achieve notable improvements of +1.16 and +1.10 BLEU scores on NIST Chinese-English and +3.83 and +3.60 ROUGE-L scores on CDC datasets, respectively. Our model also exhibits improved performance in low-data scenarios and is more adept at capturing long-distance dependencies and producing diverse outputs. This technique is also simple to integrate into existing attention models and can be readily applied to other neural translation models. Our code is available online at https://github.com/ghrua/lookahead attention. We further explore the integration of this attention model with next-sentence prediction, implying that it can be viewed as a form of bidirectional attention over the source sentence and suggesting several avenues for future research in neural machine translation. This modification allows us to revive the idealized symmetric framework by redefining the brane's state in a way that acknowledges its relationship to the geometric space. This new understanding has implications for the origins of time asymmetry, suggesting that it may stem from the brane's interaction with its surrounding geometric space rather than an intrinsic property of the brane itself. Furthermore, this concept may be applicable to multiple branes, which could result in a combination of their chemical potentials producing a variety of time-asymmetric phenomena. Lastly, we explore the connection between time-asymmetric branes and the paradox of time-asymmetric processes, which could potentially be resolved by considering the branes' production process, their initial conditions, or their difference in time-asymmetric parameters. Additionally, we examine the possibility that our time-asymmetric branes could provide insights into addressing the cosmological parity anomaly. Finally, we consider the scope of the parities discussed in this work, which are closely linked to the branes' scalar fields, and we explore the idea that other physical systems governed by different field types may exhibit parity-anomaly phenomena as well. Nonetheless, the key to solving these problems may lie in further developing the theoretical models used to describe time-asymmetric branes. Ultimately, a deeper understanding of these branes could offer a glimpse into resolving some of the most enduring challenges in physics today. Elastography, an advancing imaging technique, allows the non-invasive visualisation of tissue pathologies by identifying the physical properties of tissues. Accurate estimation of mechanical properties relies on precise measurement of tissue displacement in multiple directions. Notwithstanding advancements in elastography, the axial measurement of displacements has been more dependable than the lateral measurement. Several factors contribute to this disparity, including the sampling frequency of ultrasound signal. This study proposes a novel technique, called Virtual Source Synthetic Aperture (VSSA), for enhancing lateral displacement estimation in elastography. VSSA combines the sampling efficiency of synthetic aperture ultrasound with the signal processing advantages of linear array ultrasound. This technique enables increased sampling frequency in the lateral direction, allowing for more precise measurement of tissue displacement. To assess the performance of VSSA, a numerical model was employed to generate synthetic data, representing various scanning configurations, including linear and synthetic aperture modes. Comparative analysis of these configurations revealed that the proposed VSSA technique yields significantly better displacement measurement results than linear and synthetic aperture approaches. Furthermore, VSSA exhibited robust performance across diverse scanning parameters, exhibiting minimal variation in measurement results. In conclusion, the introduction of VSSA represents a significant breakthrough in ultrasound elastography, capable of delivering precise lateral displacement measurement, an essential component for accurate estimation of tissue mechanical properties. This study provides a theoretical framework for the development of VSSA and presents objective, quantitative evidence of its effectiveness. Nonetheless, further research is necessary to validate the performance of this technique under real-world ultrasound imaging conditions. Our approach can also be used to identify and resolve conflicts in program modifications, as shown in a case study of Decentralized Access Control.
