This study specifically explores Boolean Ramsey numbers for posets that form V-shapes, where the arms of the V can be in ascending, descending, or random order. We examine these numbers within the Boolean lattices of size $2^n$, where $n$ represents the depth of the V-shape. Notably, we establish a lower bound for the Boolean Ramsey numbers that is achieved with random ordering, and also identify specific instances for ascending and descending orderings which result in higher values. Additionally, we observe that within the Boolean lattices of size $2^n$, the number of required copies of the V-shape posets increases in proportion to $n$ for both ascending and descending orderings. Furthermore, we introduce a new family of V-shape posets that consist of a set of $k$ discrete components, and determine the corresponding Boolean Ramsey numbers for these more general structures. Finally, we discuss an application of our findings to the study of random orderings within posets. In the context of Euclidean space, a $k$-centers clustering problem involves dividing the space into $k$ discrete regions by taking the smallest possible balls centered at the data points, where the radius is optimized to minimize the data points' farthest distance to their nearest center. This research focuses on the dynamic $k$-centers problem, where new data points are added at a constant rate and existing centers need to be updated to optimize the dispersion of the data points. Our main contribution is a new algorithm for solving this problem dynamically with $O(k\sqrt{k} \cdot 4^k)$ updates per new data point and a guaranteed cluster radius of $O(\sqrt{\log k})$ after an initial polynomial-time setup. This performance surpasses previous optimal dynamic $k$-centers solutions by achieving a significantly better dependence on $k$ and is particularly beneficial for high-dimensional data sets. Moreover, our algorithm is simple, easy to implement, and is based on a novel approach combining a new cut-tree technique and a new sampling method. This research may also provide insights for other recent publications on the cut-tree approach.  In addition, our algorithm is a general solution that can be applied to various specific data sets, such as binary data sets, where our results lead to an optimal dynamic $k$-means solution for high-dimensional data sets.  For the special case of binary data sets, our algorithm guarantees a data point farthest distance to its nearest center of $O(\log k)$, which indicates that dynamic $k$-means has an optimal solution for $k \leq 10^9$ in $O(\log k)$ approximated depth.  Furthermore, our results demonstrate the practical effectiveness of our algorithm by conducting extensive experiments on various real-world and synthetic data sets.  In particular, our results show that our proposed algorithm achieves the best known theoretical performance, and is even superior to state-of-the-art static $k$-centers algorithms for some data sets. Notably, this hierarchical framework facilitates computationally demanding applications by limiting the complexity of each individual level. Recently, deep learning techniques have gained popularity for enhancing low-dose CT images, particularly due to their impressive performance at a relatively low computational cost. A key method in this area, the unsupervised cycleGAN approach, has demonstrated great promise in restoring standard-dose CT images from low-dose images without the need for paired training data. However, the use of two neural network generators in the training process is a significant limitation, primarily because the extra generator adds complexity and memory demands. In response to these issues, we have introduced a new cycleGAN method employing a single, switchable generator. By incorporating adaptive instance normalization (AdaIN) layers, the baseline generator can efficiently be transformed into multiple output configurations, effectively mimicking the functionality of multiple generators while maintaining optimal efficiency. In our evaluation of the proposed AdaIN-Switchable CycleGAN, we found it to achieve comparable restoration results to current state-of-the-art cycleGAN methods, even while significantly reducing the model's memory consumption and training parameters. Notably, our method succeeds in restoring standard-dose images from low-dose images in just 5 cycles, rather than the typical 16 or more, without the need for paired data or additional noise injection layers. Our results demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach, and we believe our method will serve as a solid foundation for future research in the restoration of low-dose CT images. Our code has been made publicly available on GitHub at https://github.com/dgamalski/AdaIN-Switchable-CycleGAN. Additionally, we have conducted further experiments to investigate the behavior of untrained healthcare professionals in using our restored low-dose CT images for diagnostic purposes, and we found that these images compare favorably to those obtained with other deep learning restoration methods as well as the original low-dose images. Overall, our findings suggest that our cycleGAN method achieves comparable diagnostic performance to state-of-the-art deep learning approaches while significantly reducing the model's complexity and memory consumption. Our study is an initial exploration into the application of unsupervised cycleGAN methods for restoring low-dose CT images, and we have identified several areas for future research to fully explore the capabilities and limitations of these models. In particular, we plan to investigate other switchable network architectures and explore the potential of our method for integrating external data. Furthermore, we have established several key metrics for evaluating the performance of our method and will utilize these metrics in our upcoming studies. Recent successes in dialog understanding tasks can be attributed to pre-training methods with contrastive learning objectives, however current methods solely consider similar dialog samples as positive examples, forcing unrelated dialogs to be distinct. To address this issue, we introduce SPACE-2, a tree-structured pre-trained model for conversations. It combines semi-supervised contrastive pre-training to learn dialog representations and a task-specific adapter for each dataset. To begin with, we propose a novel multi-dialog contrastive loss function that classifies similar dialog groups as positive examples, thereby closing the gap between intra-group dialogs. To achieve this efficiently, we categorize dialogs based on shared attributes such as user inputs and pre-defined dialog roles. To further broaden the scope of positive examples, we establish connections between unsupervised pre-trained models and the target supervised dataset using inter-group contrastive loss. To facilitate efficient computation across diverse dialog structures, we introduce a linear transformation of the average embeddings for each sub-tree. To prevent over-extraction of simple patterns, we introduce two regularization techniques: dialog structure regularization and similarity preservation. Ultimately, our approach demonstrates superior performance compared to baseline models and the current state-of-the-art in dialog understanding tasks according to our experimental results. The code for our method has been made available at https://github.com/AlibabaResearch/DAMO-ConvAI/tree/main/space2 for reproducibility purposes. Our findings also indicate that pre-trained models perform impressively on limited-labeled datasets, surpassing models pre-trained without supervision. To verify the generalizability of our findings, we conducted additional experiments and the accompanying analysis is included in the appendix. Our approach's capability to excel in low-labeled data scenarios paves the way for further exploration in the domain of natural language understanding. To contribute to the open-source community, we have shared our dataset pre-processing techniques, specifically dialog structure construction methods, that can be applied to other datasets with similar characteristics. Moreover, our experiment setup, which incorporates a step-by-step guide on training and evaluation, is now available for reference. A common approach in video super-resolution is the recurrent structure, where the main task is processed through a series of refinement frames, with each frame obtained from an upsampled previous frame. However, this method leads to aliasing and distortion due to the upsampling of motion-blurred images. To address this issue, a non-aliasing technique called sub-pixel interpolation was developed but only considers neighboring frames with similar directions of motion. As a result, this method fails to account for more complex motion patterns, leading to artifacts in the reconstructed frames. To overcome these limitations, a new algorithm called BasicVSR++ is proposed, where the refinement frame is obtained from an accurate estimation of the blurred frame rather than the upsampled previous frame. This estimation is achieved through motion estimation and warp, resulting in a more precise reconstruction of the frame. To increase efficiency, a novel single-frame estimator was developed, which provides a direct solution to the non-aliasing reconstruction of the frame. This estimator uses a multi-layer feature of the upsampled previous frame to estimate the super-resolved frame, followed by a reverse warp to obtain the estimated blurred frame. BasicVSR++ was evaluated against state-of-the-art methods on commonly used datasets, demonstrating its superiority in video super-resolution tasks. The source code of the proposed algorithm is also made publicly available. As an additional exploration, a set of challenging video super-resolution tasks was constructed to highlight the limitations of existing approaches and the advantages of the novel estimator. These challenges demonstrate the difficulties encountered when processing videos with complex motion patterns, large scale factors, and low-quality frames. To further improve the performance on these challenging tasks, a novel loss function called structural progressive loss was introduced, aiming to preserve the structural information at each upsampled layer. However, the evaluation shows that even with this optimized loss function, the existing state-of-the-art methods continue to struggle with these challenging videos. Therefore, further research is needed to fully address these complex video super-resolution tasks. The code of the proposed algorithm BasicVSR++ is made available at https://github.com/lingcacala/BasicVSRpp. Additionally, the challenge datasets are available at https://github.com/lingcacala/VideoSuperResolutionChallenges.

Due to the development of new particle colliders like muon colliders and future circular collider projects, the traditional W-boson approximation used in existing proton colliders is no longer sufficient. As energy scales increase, the precision required for theoretical predictions grows, making the W-boson approximation less accurate and necessitating a new approach. The Efficient Vector Boson Approximation, developed in this study, offers a more precise and computationally efficient alternative, enabling reliable predictions for precision measurements and direct W-boson production at next-generation colliders. The new approach implements an off-shell extension of the W-boson approximation, combining explicit and implicit approximations to minimize numerical costs while maintaining high precision in mass and couplings predictions. As a benchmark, this approach is applied to the future circular collider but is expected to be adaptable to other muon colliders. The development of more advanced numerical tools enabled precise predictions at the integrated level, surpassing the accuracy of existing vacuum polarization treatments and lattice gauge theory calculations for certain processes. The Efficiency Vector Boson Approximation shows promising results, positioning it as a viable alternative to existing approximations and treatments for colliders. The implementation of this approach as a part of the FCC optics and detector simulation framework is also described. The code is publicly available for public use. The precision achieved by this approach justifies the use of more complex lattice gauge theory simulations, and the findings can be applied to other proton colliders, providing a viable option for the Large Hadron Collider at higher energy scales. The development of the Efficient Vector Boson Approximation and the associated code, also based on the principles outlined in this study, has led to the improvement of the lattice gauge theory predictions for the muon magnetic moment anomaly. The results indicate that the choice of optics and the precision of predictions can be optimized using the efficient vector boson approximation, leading to a breakthrough in the sensitivity of mass sensitivity to a level of 0.01 GeV. In multi-task reinforcement learning, using shared representations can greatly
benefit a learner when it comes to solving a variety of tasks. However, when
the tasks are closely matched, the benefit of sharing representations drops,
and using the same network for each task can even hinder performance. In this
study, we demonstrate that this performance decline is due to a phenomenon
called catastrophic interference, where the optimization process loses balance
between tasks. To counter this effect, we develop a novel architecture
called the Modular Multi-Task Learner, which utilizes a separate critic
network for each task. In our experiments, this architecture outperforms
existing models, showcasing its effectiveness in mitigating catastrophic
interference and enabling a learner to successfully solve a diverse set of
random MDPs and real-world challenges, including multi-task robotic navigation
and game playing. Our code is available at https://github.com/google-research/google-research/tree/main/modular_multi_task_learning. 
We further investigate the interplay between different memory capacities and
the benefit of using a hard attention mechanism in our proposed framework. 
Our results highlight the critical role of memory allocation in multi-task
learning and suggest that, in some cases, a hard attention mechanism can
diminish the benefit of using a high-capacity shared network. Ultimately, our
study provides a clear understanding of the limitations and challenges of multi-
task reinforcement learning and offers a suite of efficient, memory-aware models
that can effectively learn from experience when faced with a diverse range of
tasks. Additionally, we explore the implications of our findings for other
effortless generalization phenomena in machine learning and suggest the value of
conducting a more in-depth examination of the relationship between optimization
balance and the variety of tasks. This study is a strong starting point for
delving deeper into the complex relationship between optimization balance, the
variability of tasks, and the effectiveness of multi-task reinforcement learning. 
We believe that our work will serve as a solid foundation for conducting a
more in-depth examination of these critical aspects in the field of multi-task
reinforcement learning.

more light on the intricate connection between optimization balance and the
diversity of tasks, as well as the best practices for designing efficient,
memory-aware models for multi-task reinforcement learning.

This paper formulates the Three Balls Conjecture in terms of a given function satisfying a specific property, and provides a proof for a subset of functions satisfying this property. The conjecture in question concerns the ability to determine, based on knowledge of a function's values on the surfaces of three non-intersecting balls, whether it has a zero interior to one of the balls. The focus here is on a type of function derived from the Dirac operator, particularly within the context of Clifford analysis. We establish that harmonic functions in higher-dimensional space can be used to prove the conjecture, and further demonstrate that functions representing polynomials also satisfy the conjecture's conditions. However, we also identify instances where the conjecture is known to be false, suggesting its validity is dependent on specific characteristics of the function in question. The primary approach to proving the conjecture involves expressing a function's behavior on the balls' surfaces in terms of their radii and the relationship between the balls themselves. A key aspect of this proof includes introducing an important distance metric measuring the balls' external distance, and demonstrating how this understanding enables the prediction of a function's behavior on the balls' surfaces. The proof provided covers the case of three distinct balls with equal radii, and leaves open the question of whether this result holds for balls with non-equal radii. The implications of this work for the broader scope of the Three Balls Conjecture are also discussed. Additionally, we explore connections between this conjecture and other problems, including the well-known Beurling-Malliavin theorem and Carleman's estimate, and identify instances where the conjecture is known to be false, notably in the context of functions derived from the Laplace-Beltrami operator. This is crucial in imaging techniques such as MRI, computed tomography, deblurring and super-resolution, among others. Because there can be multiple plausible images given the measurements and prior information, the focus isn't solely on recovering a single ideal solution, but rather on constructing a probability distribution that incorporates all possible outcomes. To this end, we propose a novel framework using a regularized conditional Wasserstein GAN that achieves this by treating the image reconstruction as a sampling process. We also explore two specific applications - one is for treating noisy measurements, the other is for recovering images from partial observations with known occlusions. We show that our method outperforms existing approaches in these scenarios. We further provide an analytical solution for one part and an efficient iterative method for solving the other. This article examines the possibility of finding invariant surfaces in fractional order dynamical systems. To achieve this, we first establish a condition for a surface to be invariant by expressing the dynamical system in polar coordinates and the surface in question using the parameterization method. We then analyze the relationship between this condition and the system's stability. Subsequent to identifying the necessary condition for the existence of an invariant surface, we demonstrate that this condition is also sufficient in a specific context. However, we also identify cases where the condition is not met, resulting in the nonexistence of invariant surfaces. These instances include a fractionally ordered Chua's circuit and the fractional order dynamical system presented by Yenoudi et al. in their study of robust control surface implementation. These examples demonstrate that the proposed condition for the existence of an invariant surface is applicable across a broader class of dynamical systems than previously considered. Moreover, we establish that the key factor determining the presence or absence of an invariant surface is the difference between the stability of the system along its radial and tangential directions. This conclusion leads to a previously hidden connection between the specified condition and the system's stability along these separate directions. Finally, we explore the implications of our findings for control surface design in fractional order dynamical systems. While the proposed condition provides insight into the existence of invariant surfaces, it is not a sufficient guarantee for the surface's effectiveness in these systems. Therefore, numerical testing is necessary to assess the performance of a controlled system. Additionally, we highlight that the approach presented can be adapted to a wider class of dynamical systems, encompassing those defined by first-order differential equations. High-sensitivity radio telescopes allowing real-time data processing have made possible a new method of investigating the interstellar medium by analyzing the pulse patterns of highly energetic pulsars. This approach, pulse profile scintillometry, enables researchers to gain a deeper understanding of the medium's small-scale structures across the line of sight to the pulsar. By studying the Earth's velocity of scintillation pattern and frequency, researchers can determine the local standard of rest and the characteristics of the medium's component "cells". This specific study on the pulsar B1133+16, conducted at radio telescopes in Arecibo, Puerto Rico and Green Bank, West Virginia, yielded information on the medium's properties between 1.4 and 3.0 GHz and provided a 3D map of the line of sight to the pulsar. The findings indicate a presence of dense plasma within a few astronomical units of the pulsar and also reveal a "cell" with a large linear size in the direction perpendicular to the solar motion. This discovery may be related to the Earth's orbit crossing over a dense boundary in the medium, potentially affecting transverse components of the solar wind. This study on B1133+16 contributes significantly to the growing collection of data on the interstellar medium and pulsar environments and may provide a basis for further investigation of this particular "cell" and its relation to the medium's larger structure. This study was performed in collaboration with the Arecibo Observatory's Group for Advancement of Physics and Engineering and the National Radio Astronomy Observatory's GBT. It also highlights the capabilities of real-time data processing at radio telescopes allowing direct detection of scintillometry phenomena. This study was published in the journal Astrophysical Journal Supplement Series, volume 243, issue 1. Additionally, this study was mentioned in an article featured in the Journals Highlights section and in the Arecibo Observatory's newspaper, Voz del Observatorio. This study was also presented at the 2008 Arecibo Meeting on Pulsar Astronomy and presented at the 40th Leiden Meeting on Coordination Chemistry. This paper presents a generative model called Quasi-Periodic WaveNet (QPNet) to enhance the limited pitch control of WaveNet (WN) through pitch-dependent expanded convolution neural networks. WN achieves realism by modeling sound waveforms as a series of overlapping collections of signals related in time and space, however its effectiveness is hampered by its lack of explicit representation of spectral patterns. This shortcoming is addressed in QPNet by integrating pitch-dependent expanded convolutions into the autoregressive Raw Waveform Generative Model, allowing the model to capture spectral patterns based on quasi-periodic signals of varying durations and frequencies. The implementation of a single-dimensional quadratic function predicts global pitch period and local amplitude, thereby informing two types of expanded convolutions. Despite its complex architecture comprising hundreds of millions of parameters, QPNet exhibits superior performance and efficiency compared to current TTS methods like WaveNet, Transformable WaveNet, and Parallel WaveNet, matching the quality of generated audio while requiring a mere 5% of their parameter count. The model's ability to balance high-fidelity audio generation with low latency is a significant advantage. The source code of QPNet is available online at the specified URL. The model's capacity to produce high-quality audio in low-latency mode makes it suitable for real-time music composition and other music generation applications. The paper also contains a novel music composition method called QPNet-based Music Composition, which generates polyphonic music by activating specific model parameters in response to multiple melodic lines. The model's performance in these applications is evaluated and the results are presented in the form of audio files available on online repositories. The paper introduces a new evaluation metric called Model Diversity, which assesses the diversity of audio generated by different model iterations. The paper contains additional compositions created with the QPNet model, and the sound quality of the generated audio is subject to the listening test of a group of music experts. The test reveals that while the model's audio is perceived as realistic by the experts, they can distinguish it from human-performance audio. The paper includes additional quantitative measurements of the model's performance, including a comparison of the model's quality, diversity, and latency against current state-of-the-art WaveNet variants. The results show that the paper's approach yields a model with enhanced quality, diversity, and latency in all measurement categories. The paper contains an appendix with additional details on the listening test, the model's latency measurement, and the evaluation of the paper's experiments. The paper is suitable for presentation at the ICASSP conference

Many researchers use online annotation tools to gather datasets for various NLP tasks. However, the majority of these tools are designed with a single-purpose interface, requiring annotators to mark multiple attributes for each text sample separately. This can lead to reduced productivity and decreased quality due to the repeated process of re-entering identical information for different feature annotations. To address these issues, our team has developed a unique web platform called MADARi, allowing for the simultaneous annotation of Arabic morphological characteristics and spelling correction. This approach streamlines the annotation process by incorporating a preformatted text area that displays the structure of an Arabic sentence, thereby facilitating faster and more accurate annotations. Furthermore, to enhance the usability of our tool, we have incorporated an innovative feature that generates a sorted list of all text samples used for annotation, making it easier for supervisors to monitor the progress of annotators. Additionally, we have incorporated a user management system to oversee the annotation process, as well as a data storage section that retains the annotated data in a format suitable for further NLP applications. To increase the efficiency of our web platform, we have included a robust backend infrastructure using a microservice architecture. This architecture enables a high traffic capacity for the web application, as evidenced by the positive feedback received from over 500 registered users who have successfully utilized our tool to gather more than 20,000 annotated sentence datasets. Our web platform is an open-source, publicly accessible system available at https://madari.seas.gwu.edu. Additionally, we have explored the usability of our web platform through a comprehensive usability study, detailing our methodological approach and the results obtained. This study has yielded valuable insights to improve the design of our web application, as well as insights that can be applied to a broader range of similar annotation tools. Planets within the habitable zone of their stars, if they possess thick atmospheres, may not be suitable for life as previously assumed. This study addresses this concern by examining how gas ladened atmospheres on temperate exoplanets interact with their stars. It focuses particularly on K2-22b, a world that orbits an M-dwarf star and falls within the star's habitable zone. However, this exoplanet is twice as large as Neptune and suffers from tidal locking. By utilizing the ExoMastro modeling tool, we explored how its atmosphere could be affected by the star's energy for different atmospheric conditions. This helped to identify a possible atmospheric composition based on spectroscopic data from the Hubble Space Telescope. Subsequently, a simulation of this exoplanet's transit spectrum revealed the potential for its atmosphere to be gas ladened, which could still harbor life. This finding highlights the importance of considering atmospheric thickness when identifying potentially habitable exoplanets. It also emphasizes the value of using stellar energy models in combination with observational data and theoretical atmosphere simulations to gain a more comprehensive understanding of these distant worlds. This approach can refine our definition of a habitable exoplanet and provide a new framework for evaluating its life-supporting potential. Furthermore, it is crucial for guiding future resource allocation in telescope time and observational missions like the James Webb Space Telescope. Its use cases include studying temperate exoplanets within the orbit of small stars, which are thought to be the most promising for detecting biosignatures. Additionally, this study demonstrates how to select the most suitable stellar energy models, choose the best atmospheric models, and simulate transit spectra for optimized data interpretation. This involves using a comprehensive modeling framework that considers various model assumptions and their implications for observational predictions. The increased resistance in this setup significantly alters tunneling conductance, impacting it in distinct ways. While the Majorana peak persists in rising as temperatures decrease in proportion to T^(2r-1), with r defined as the exponential product of the resistance and a universal constant divided by the Planck's constant (all values below 1/2), non-Majorana-induced zero-energy peaks fragment into two separate peaks at non-zero temperatures, displaying varying conductance in relation to temperature by way of a power law. Furthermore, tunneling associated with a Majorana mode falls within the same broad class of universal behaviors as does the case for unstable critical points with a non-Majorana mode. The development of advanced detection algorithms through deep learning has accelerated the identification of road defects, but their effectiveness is highly dependent on high-resolution images collected from multiple sources, including drones, vehicles, and smartphones. To streamline the process, a comprehensive platform called RoadAtlas has been developed, providing an intuitive interface for users to capture and annotate images of road conditions and attaching metadata to these annotations. This platform leverages deep learning algorithms, specifically fast object detection methods, to pinpoint potential road issues from the user-provided data, even in the absence of comprehensive training datasets. To facilitate collaboration and transparency, RoadAtlas features interactive visualization tools, allowing users and industry experts to review and validate the predicted results alongside the underlying model predictions and grass-roots annotations. Furthermore, this platform generates detailed reports highlighting predicted issues, model performance, and user-provided feedback. To accommodate various use cases, RoadAtlas offers a customizable workflow that enables users to select specific detection tasks, select models for evaluation, and integrate results into the dashboard for easy review. Additionally, this platform provides a centralized repository for managing annotated datasets, comprising a robust dataset management system that enables users to import, organize, and export annotated data in popular formats, such as COCO and VBIS. By integrating leading deep learning libraries, including TensorFlow and PyTorch, RoadAtlas enables researchers and practitioners to explore cutting-edge detection approaches, as well as facilitate the exploration of various performance evaluation metrics, including precision, recall, and AUC-ROC. This intelligent platform is designed to streamline the road flaw detection process, accelerate innovation, and introduce its features to the broader community through its user-friendly interface and comprehensive documentation, available at https://roadatlas.org/. This work has been recognized with an award at the 2022 IEEE Conference on Intelligent Transportation Systems, System Integration, and Information and Telecommunication Technologies. The seven-dimensional supergravity theory, often referred to as the M-theory's heart, can be expressed through an extension of type II string theory in ten dimensions.  We investigate the bicategorical structure underlying this relationship and find that the heart of M-theory corresponds to a marked bicategory derived from a combination of the type II string theory's bicategory and a particular interaction bicategory connected through'shadows'.  This analysis provides physical context to previous mathematical findings and establishes a connection between the type II string theory's surface prologue and shadows.  We also establish that the type II string theory's surface prologue can be interpreted as a category of Chord diagrams arising from a particular combination of the heart of M-theory and the fermionic type II string theory's surface prologue.  This relationship demonstrates how the heart of M-theory interacts with the fermionic type II string theory's surface prologue through shadows.  We further show that the heart of M-theory includes a bicategorical mirror symmetry associated with a particular gradient flow in a landscape of vacua, and that this symmetry results in a combination of the type II string theory's surface prologue and the fermionic type II string theory's surface prologue experiencing a categorical Markov Process.  This process maintains the category's global properties, ensuring that the type II string theory's surface prologue and the fermionic type II string theory's surface prologue remain connected and mirror-symmetric.  We also introduce the concept of 'Shadows' as lagrangian correspondences that generate the heart of M-theory, and demonstrate that the heart of M-theory can be expressed as a combination of the type II string theory's surface prologue and the fermionic type II string theory's surface prologue connected through'shadows'.  We further show that the'shadows' effect gives rise to the generation of the M-theory's heart from the type II string theory's surface prologue and the fermionic type II string theory's surface prologue, and that this generation process results in the extension of the type II string theory's surface prologue's higher symmetry by a categorical version of the M-theory's heart's higher symmetry. Our investigation discloses an unsettling phenomenon affecting state-of-the-art visual noise localization models. When trained on a combination of clean images and noisily labeled data, they surprisingly exhibit a critical flaw: they are incapable of accurately identifying the areas of image modification. This unexpected limitation becomes especially pronounced when noisier labels are utilized in the training process. Our findings indicate that this shortfall arises due to the model's tendency to give precedence to simplistically identifying the overall image classification over precise position encoding. As a result, we propose a more challenging evaluation framework that prioritizes precise position encoding, aiming to enhance noise robustness and position sensitivity. To achieve this, we introduce two novel evaluation metrics: the accurate position recall and the harmonic mean of accuracy and false positive rate. Our proposed framework serves as a rigorous test of a model's ability to effectively process visual noises with complex layouts, incorporating various types of positional misalignments, rotations, and scaling. Ultimately, our results demonstrate that models passed through this rigorous evaluation pipeline exhibit significantly improved noise robustness and position sensitivity, outperforming those that only excel in classification tasks. When subjected to our challenging evaluation protocol, models that excel at visual noise classification often struggle to scale or rotate noises accurately. In contrast, models that excel at our proposed evaluation protocol showcase excellent performance across all evaluation metrics, demonstrating our framework's effectiveness in promoting robust noise position awareness. As a result, we are able to enhance the performance of state-of-the-art visual noise classification models while reducing their reliance on overfitting techniques, resulting in a notable improvement in accurate position recall from 20.3% to 55.8%. Most importantly, we find that these improvements are equally applicable to models trained with abundant data, demonstrating the broad applicability of our proposed evaluation protocol. In addition to presenting our findings, we also contribute a more challenging evaluation protocol that encompasses a comprehensive set of visual noise position sensitivity evaluation protocols. This comprehensive evaluation protocol encompasses diverse scenarios of positional misalignment, rotations, and scaling, encompassing 36 distinct configurations. We believe this comprehensive evaluation protocol will serve as a benchmark for benchmarking the position sensitivity of visual noise localization models. Graph neural networks (GNNs) have excelled in various tasks due to their flexibility in handling complex and dynamic graph data. Current GNN models operate within a Euclidean framework but have a significant limitation - they cannot effectively represent time and other directional relationships. Our proposal, Lorentzian GNNs, breaks through this constraint by introducing a new relational modeling framework rooted in differential geometry. Lorentzian GNNs treat graphs as topological structures embedded in a differential manifold and leverage their intrinsic geometric properties to enhance GNN performance. Our approach is highly versatile, making it compatible with existing GNN architectures by simply replacing their convolutional modules with Lorentzian counterparts. Our experiments demonstrate substantial improvements over traditional GNNs, and we are exploring applications in social network analysis and temporal data processing. Furthermore, our findings show that in certain circumstances, including the scenario where the Young diagram of the corresponding Schur polynomial satisfies a specific shifting property, the matrix entries of the quantum immanents can be reinterpreted as structured versions of shifted Schur polynomials. These findings provide valuable insights for discovering new phenomena in 4d and 5d transition metal oxides. We introduce FastEpoched, an open-source C++/Python library for computing definite integrals related to Green's functions in two-dimensional Euclidean space. Our focus is on linear operators, including div(ABu) for matrices A and B, with Euclidean and non-Euclidean kernels available. FastEpoched achieves high performance by utilizing numerical methods including the quadrature, stochastic fragmentation, and quasi-random sampling of integrals. Our experiments show significant speed-ups, with performance gains being particularly noticeable in large-scale simulations beyond 10,000 particles. FastEpoched has an easy-to-use interface and is adaptable to various applications, including projects like SwiftNewton and SwiftStochastic. We have made FastEpoched available under an permissive license to facilitate its integration into other projects. Our results also demonstrate the efficacy of quasi-random sampling, which we found to be relevant to a broader range of applications than we initially anticipated. We have decided to release FastEpoched as an independent library to give other researchers the opportunity to build upon our contributions.
